articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed distances himself from Hasan Piker’s comments on Israel and Jewish Americans
articles.summary: El-Sayed, the Senate Democratic nominee in Michigan, appeared with Piker at campaign events during the primary season.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, distanced himself Monday from progressive commentator Hasan Piker, who suggested that some pro-Israel rhetoric may lead to backlash against American Jews. The controversy could complicate El-Sayed’s campaign as he tries to unify Democrats in a battleground state that will help decide control of the U.S. Senate. El Sayed is one of several Democratic candidates this year who harnessed Piker’s online megaphone to appeal to younger voters, and they appeared together at campaign events during the primary, but last week’s comments may have cooled the relationship. Wearing a suit and tie during one of his typically hours-long livestreams, Piker argued against the idea that opposing Israel is antisemitic. American Jews are not uniformly supportive of Israel, he said, but many “Jewish institutions” are “teaching people the idea that Jews are monolithic” and “its a very dangerous mode of propaganda.” “If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel mind you, but against American Jews,” he said. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat, issued a sharply critical statement. “The malicious claim that American Jews are inviting violence against themselves is dangerous and antisemitic,” he said on social media. “There is zero justification for threats against the safety of our Jewish brothers and sisters at a moment of rising hate.” El-Sayed issued his own statement later in the day. “I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence,” he said. “This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past.” He also said “antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms” and “nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople.” “And while politicians and pundits try to make this race about a Twitch streamer, we’re going to be talking about gas, groceries, good schools and healthcare,” El-Sayed added. While Piker was speaking on the livestream last week, he was displaying an X post with a photo of Jeremy Moss, a Jewish Democratic candidate for U.S. House in Michigan, on his screen. Moss posted Monday, “I will not be lectured by a California podcaster about what Oakland County, Michigan’s Jewish community should and shouldn’t believe,” adding that “we certainly won’t be gaslit that we’re responsible for the antisemitic harm upon us.” Piker’s spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. On another livestream Monday, he called El-Sayed’s statement “neutral” and described the outrage as a “smear.” He argued that he wasn’t advocating violence but warning against the rhetoric that could. El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former congressman Mike Rogers, said El-Sayed’s response was inadequate. “El-Sayed doesn’t have the guts to disavow his running mate,” Rogers said. He said the Democratic nominee is “unfit to represent our state.” Piker’s previous statements has been controversial, including a past comment that “Hamas is a thousand times better” than Israel. Some Democrats urged El-Sayed to go further in responding to Piker’s comments. “I want Abdul to win desperately, but the most predictable thing in the world was that Piker would inevitably become a serious liability in a general election,” Tré Easton, a Democratic strategist, wrote on social media. “If you care about Abdul’s campaign succeeding, you should want him to distance himself from Piker clearly and directly.”

articles.title: Trump’s theory of global power faces a reckoning in Iran and Canada
articles.summary: Donald Trump’s presidency rests on the premise that he and the United States are so powerful that allies and enemies alike must submit to his will.
articles.body: Donald Trump’s presidency rests on the premise that he and the United States are so powerful that allies and enemies alike must submit to his will. His break with decades of US foreign policy doctrine is laced through his speeches and national security strategies. It was best explained in January by top aide Stephen Miller, who told CNN’s Jake Tapper that “iron laws” dictate a real world that is “governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power.” But the philosophy faces its most serious tests in deepening showdowns with Iran and Canada. Iran has defied the might of the US military for six months in a war Trump started but has been unable to end. Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney, who shut down trade talks with Washington, has meanwhile argued more forcefully than any other Western leader that the US under Trump “has changed.” He told his country Saturday that Trump was using “economic integration as a weapon.” It is a commentary on the extreme disruption of the Trump era that Canada, one of America’s most loyal friends, has found itself in a similar state of economic warfare with the US as Iran, one of Washington’s worst foes. But the Trump administration left no doubt Monday what it wants as it fights a trade war with Ottawa and a shooting war with Tehran. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an “economic onslaught” against Iran’s global financial connections, drawing an analogy with the D-Day invasion that turned the tide in World War II. Trump, meanwhile warned on social media that “The U.S.A. will always be far bigger, richer, and stronger than Canada.” He added: “Someone should get these clowns to ‘fall in line.’” Will Trump stay the course? The administration’s rhetoric Monday suggests that Trump is now sending the US economy to war. Trump hopes to chalk up a lopsided trade deal with Canada and to finally bring about the downfall of Iran’s regime. But the way forward is uncertain on both fronts because the president often backs down when the economic consequences of his attempts to assert his authority become clear. Any prolonged US effort to prevail over Canada and Iran — and third-party nations sanctioned in his bid to shut down Tehran’s financial networks — could trigger retaliation that causes energy and food price hikes for US consumers. It could also rattle US markets at a time when some investors fear a bond crisis. If Monday’s threats are the precursor to more TACOs (“Trump always chickens out”), the president will undermine his own power and the nation’s, and slip closer to lame-duck status as difficult midterm elections loom in November. What Trump could achieve by strangling Iran’s economy Bessent’s announcement was the latest US effort to find a new way out of the war with Iran. But the D-Day analogy seemed tonally off, given the terrible sacrifices made by American soldiers to liberate Europe. And unlike Bessent, allied commander Gen. Dwight Eisenhower didn’t spent days in 1944 previewing a massive attack only to follow through with new threats of sanctions and no timeline. Still, administration skeptics often ignore the genuine power that Trump could wield by clever use of economic warfare. A truly global effort to cut off Iran’s pathways to finance and trade could inflict extreme damage on an already devastated economy. “It can work if we can get the buy-in of our partners,” Max Meizlish, a former senior Treasury official, said on CNN News Central Monday, specifically referring to Bank Melli, an Iranian commercial bank controlled by the government that operates in France, Germany and elsewhere and is a cog in Iran’s efforts to evade sanctions. Kenneth Rogoff, a former IMF chief economist who is now a Harvard University chair, told CNN’s Richard Quest: “Fundamentally, sanctions work if you can get most of the world behind you. But if they’re not, it’s very hard.” Trump might have had more success with such an approach before alienating US allies with a war many regard as unwise and illegal. And the White House may be misreading its capacity to influence events inside Tehran. Signs of disagreement between pragmatists and hardliners over the economy are encouraging. But Washington has for decades over-read such tea leaves and assumed regime collapse would follow. Most damagingly, the Trump administration is sending signals that it may not be serious about its own policy. There was no immediate action against an array of Chinese banks that facilitate Beijing’s trade in cut-price Iranian oil. China has already said it will defend its interests — code for potential retaliatory reaction against the US that could further raise prices and anger US voters. It showed last year in threatening to curtail rare earth mineral exports critical to the US defense and tech industries that it can counter Trump’s power. And the US leader also has a big date circled on his calendar — the state visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping next month. It’s hard to see him souring the atmosphere before then. In a revealing moment, Bessent only reinforced doubts about the administration’s staying power. He was asked why he was not immediately imposing secondary sanctions on entities that deal with Iran. “Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior; why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he replied. Canada sees a showdown that goes beyond a trade dispute The administration is less wary of sanctioning the manufacturers of Canadian hockey sticks than Chinese banks. And cross-border rhetoric is increasingly toxic. “We have to remember, Canada is a state. Sorry, Freudian slip. That was actually an accident,” Vice President JD Vance said Monday. Ontario Premier Doug Ford said at a news conference that “I have a lot of real estate on my ass, so (Trump) has a lot of room to kiss my ass.” Venting can sometimes create political room to relaunch talks. But Canadians believe they are embroiled in more than a trade dispute. Drew Dilkens, the mayor of Windsor, Ontario, just across from Detroit, explained the damage inflicted by Trump’s 51st-state claims. “When you say it the first time, perhaps you can laugh it off, but it was the doubling down and certainly continuing to reinforce that,” he told CNN’s Brianna Keilar. Ottawa said that, among other disputes, Carney ended trade talks after the US sought to water down its constitutional guarantees of bilingualism. Printing packaging for products sold in Canada in French as well as English is an inconvenience for US firms. But it’s a validation of the cultural and linguistic diversity that keeps Canada whole. Carney also implied Washington sought to restrict trade deals that his government could make with third countries. “We will not allow any nation to dictate our future,” Carney said Saturday. As the smaller economy, Canada would suffer the most harm in a trade war with the US. But it can challenge American power. A long tariff duel could result in the mutually assured destruction of the auto industry on both sides of the border. And the growing impact of Canadian boycotts could weaken Republicans in key contests in border states Michigan and Maine, which could decide who controls the US Senate next year. And in seeking to impose his dominance, Trump may have revealed another iron law of power that Miller did not mention back in January. When people see their sovereignty and independence threatened by a hostile greater power, there is almost no price they will not pay.

articles.title: South Carolina could give Trump a revitalizing win — or his most embarrassing loss
articles.summary: The runoff to succeed the late Sen. Lindsey Graham will reveal whether the president can propel a virtual stranger to the Senate.
articles.body:
Donald Trump is facing one of his biggest tests of the midterms — and it's of his own making.

The president has spent a significant amount of time and money trying to help Sen. Darline Graham defeat Rep. Ralph Norman in Tuesday's snap GOP Senate primary. He's done more for Graham than he has for the battleground Republicans whose general election fights will determine control of Congress: Not only did he push her to run for a full term , he also held a rare in-person rally for her and tapped into his MAGA Inc. warchest during the final days of the race.

If, after lending all that support, Graham fails, it would be Trump's most embarrassing loss of the cycle. A win, however, would let him flex his ability to power an unknown political figure to office.

"If Darline does come up short, it would be just a massive, massive embarrassment to the White House and to the president. Just an utter rejection," said Matthew Bartlett, a Republican strategist and former Trump State Department appointee during his first term.

Tuesday's runoff to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham on the November ballot won't meaningfully affect the balance of power in Washington. What it will do is reveal the extent of Trump's clout, because of just how much personal political capital he has expended in the race to convince voters to elect a virtual stranger.

"The fact that he came to the state on short notice to do a rally, and we haven't seen that in a lot of endorsements, I think that sends a very strong message that he's all in," said Andrew Boucher, a GOP strategist and chair of South Carolina's Charleston County Republican Party, who is neutral in the race.

Trump has framed the race as nothing less than a referendum on himself. Rallying with Graham in Myrtle Beach last week, the president told voters to "pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot."

On Monday, a Federal Election Commission report revealed that Trump's super PAC had spent $827,000 on text messages and phone calls for Graham. It's one of the largest expenditures this cycle from MAGA Inc., and cash that Republicans in battlegrounds are anxiously awaiting for themselves.

One national Republican operative, who was granted anonymity to candidly discuss the president's influence on the race, noted just how far Trump's support has gotten Graham: "She wouldn't even be in this place if she didn't have [his support]. The outside help she's had has kind of made this competitive."

Before GOP Gov. Henry McMaster appointed her to serve out the remainder of her late brother's term in July, Graham was a complete political novice. Graham has worked for the South Carolina Vocational Rehabilitation Department and has led the Commission for the Blind since 2019, but she had never held or even sought public office — a fact that her opponents have attacked her for repeatedly on the campaign trail, especially after she stumbled over a key foreign policy question on the debate stage earlier this month. Her clearest connection to electoral politics lay solely in being the late senator's younger sister.

Trump's past mistakes in South Carolina loom over the race. The Senate primary has echoes of the state's governor's contest earlier this summer, in which Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette, a little-known Trump-backed candidate, fell to the more well-known Attorney General Alan Wilson. As public polling began to show Evette trailing significantly in the first days of that runoff, Trump issued a rare dual endorsement to include Wilson .

Evette's defeat, coupled with a batch of uncharacteristic losses by Trump endorsees in GOP primaries in Georgia, Iowa, Minnesota, Wyoming and Michigan, has put all the more attention on Graham.

The power of his endorsement is on the president's own mind, too. In a Sunday night post on Truth Social , Trump mused that his "Endorsements are stronger than ever," pointing to splashy charts comparing his wins to his comparatively few defeats.

But in the same breath, he acknowledged that his power is not always absolute: "The few that lost were done out of loyalty. It was almost impossible for them to win but, I felt obligated to go with them because they were, in my opinion, good people!"

When asked for comment, a White House spokesperson pointed to specific remarks from Trump's speech at Friday's rally with Graham, including his acknowledgement that he urged her to jump in the primary.

"She's never done it before, but she knows politics well," Trump told supporters on Myrtle Beach. "She loves our military. She loves things that have to do with greatness for America."

Graham's foreign policy debate flub — in which she said "national security is not my thing" in response to a question of U.S. interests in Taiwan — revealed the pitfalls of running for office with no prior experience. Norman has taken advantage of that stumble by hammering her inexperience.

The closing stretch of the race has been characterized by Graham trying to tie herself to Trump and burnish her conservative credentials across the state. Norman has tried to shore up support in his Upstate stronghold and expand into the Low Country where former Gov. Mark Sanford — who endorsed his campaign late last week — dominated in the first round. Norman's also taken to Fox News to bash Graham as an "unknown" and "propped-up candidate."

Graham's campaign hopes to consolidate support from Rep. Russell Fry's (R-S.C.) district after he endorsed her campaign a few days into the runoff. Her closing ad of the race claims Norman "turned his back on Trump's agenda" and is interspersed with footage of her on the rally stage alongside the president.

The GOP party establishment in South Carolina has fallen in line behind Graham.

Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) publicly backed her bid on the first day of the runoff, Evette got in line shortly thereafter and McMaster followed several days later.

Graham's campaign has itself spent just over $1 million in ads since the outset of the race, but that spending is bolstered by at least three other outside groups — including Security is Strength PAC, Palmetto Action PAC, and American Mission PAC — who also supported her late brother's primary bid earlier this year. Their spending has topped $6 million, according to AdImpact.

Norman has had his own outside help from a notable figure and longtime ally: Former U.N. Ambassador Nikki Haley and her aligned groups have spent more than $700,000 for Norman, including $200,000 on a supportive ad from her issue advocacy group, Stand for America.

But that's still much lower compared with what Graham has received.

"Sen. Scott engaging in the race, the congressional delegation, all these portions of it. Congressman Fry engaging in the race is a big deal. You could almost say that's the opposite of what you had in the governor's race," said a South Carolina-based Republican operative, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly and is staying neutral in the race.

Spokespeople for Graham and Norman did not respond to requests for comment.

Graham is still somewhat dogged by her high-profile debate stage mistake, though she's tried to redirect the attention in interviews.

"You know what I've done in the last week? I've gone around this entire state talking to as many people as I possibly can. And you know how many of them brought up Taiwan and national security? Not one!" she said at a press conference in Columbia on Monday.

The late August runoff date could prove unpredictable for both candidates as they seek to drive out their supporters across the state. The twilight of South Carolina's sticky, slow summer is in full effect: Most kids have returned to school, families across the state are packing their beach gear for one final getaway and the doldrums of summer are still in full force.

Several Republicans said that could mean a lower turnout — which could be a boon for a known-quantity candidate with a long history in local office, like Norman.

"A lot of the candidates that have defeated Trump-endorsed folks across the map this cycle, they're well-known entities," said the national GOP operative. "It's hard to overcome some of the basics of politics, where name ID goes a long way. Familiarity with the candidate matters. Having a favorable view and someone who aligns with your values more matters, even if there's a Trump endorsement."

Samuel Benson contributed to this report.

articles.title: Polls close in Oklahoma as Trump-backed candidate faces GOP runoff
articles.summary: Republican primary runoffs in South Carolina and Oklahoma put Trump's endorsement record on the line after five gubernatorial picks fell short this cycle.
articles.body: The polls have closed in Oklahoma, South Carolina and Georgia as President Donald Trump's clout over the GOP and the immense power of his endorsements in Republican primaries are on the line Tuesday in statewide runoff elections in South Carolina and Oklahoma. Trump is backing Sen. Darline Graham in the Republican Senate nomination runoff in South Carolina, in the race to succeed her late brother, GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham, who unexpectedly died this summer at age 71. And the president is supporting former state budget secretary and former state Sen. Mike Mazzei for the Republican gubernatorial nomination in Oklahoma, where GOP Gov. Kevin Stitt is term-limited. Both Trump-backed candidates are facing off in competitive contests on that day that also includes a special election runoff in Georgia to fill a congressional seat left vacant following Democratic Rep. David Scott’s death in April. The two candidates are Democrats, which means the winner will further reduce an already extremely fragile Republican majority in the House. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB In South Carolina, Darline Graham is facing off with conservative Rep. Ralph Norman, with the winner replacing the late senator as the Republican Senate nominee on the midterm ballot in reliably red South Carolina. Graham and Norman finished first and second in a special Senate primary two weeks ago, but with neither candidate landing a majority of the vote, they advanced to a runoff from a field that also included Rep. Russell Fry and former governor and former Rep. Mark Sanford. "We need every South Carolina patriot to go to the polls and vote for Darline Graham," Trump urged on Friday as he headlined a rally for Graham in Myrtle Beach. "What I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot. Just come and vote. It's so important." Graham is backed by term-limited South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster, who last month appointed her to fulfill the rest of her late brother's current term in the Senate. She also has the backing of Fry, a top Trump ally in the House, as well as the support of Sen. Tim Scott, South Carolina's other senator and chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee. WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM RACES SHOW Norman, who unsuccessfully campaigned earlier this year for the GOP gubernatorial nomination in the race to succeed McMaster, has been showcasing his support for the president in his Senate campaign and questioning Trump's backing of Darline Graham. He was backed last week by Sanford, who briefly launched a long-shot and unsuccessful 2020 presidential challenge against Trump. Sanford, who is known as a fiscally conservative budget hawk, pointed to the nation's debt as a key motivator behind his decision to launch a Senate campaign, and later for backing Norman. The Trump endorsement hasn't proven to be a sure bet this cycle in South Carolina. Trump backed Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette for the GOP gubernatorial nomination — in the race to succeed the term-limited McMaster — ahead of the state's early June primary. Evette was the top vote-getter in the primary but lost the ensuing runoff election against South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson in a landslide. And Trump, ever hungry for a victory, endorsed Wilson in addition to Evette days before the runoff. "It’s becoming a referendum on Trump," a South Carolina-based Republican consultant told Fox News Digital. The strategist, who asked for anonymity to speak more freely, argued Trump "came to South Carolina to solidify his endorsement because he has to show a win here." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Norman, as he runs for the Senate, is also backed by former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley, who served as ambassador to the United Nations during Trump's first term in the White House. Norman was the only member of South Carolina's congressional delegation, and the first member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, to endorse Haley over Trump in the 2024 Republican presidential primaries. "Trump still has a nasty taste in his mouth for Nikki Haley," the GOP strategist argued. In Oklahoma, the Trump-backed Mazzei finished slightly behind state Attorney General Gentner Drummond in the initial June GOP primary, with a crowded field keeping either from winning the nomination outright. The winner of Tuesday's GOP runoff will be considered the clear general election favorite in the Republican-dominated state. HEAD HERE FOR THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLLS IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS Trump has boasted a powerful endorsement scorecard in GOP primaries so far this election cycle. "My Endorsements are stronger than ever," the president touted this past weekend in a social media post. But five of his gubernatorial picks in Republican primaries have fallen short. Besides South Carolina's Evette, that list includes Georgia Lt. Gov. Burt Jones and Rep. Randy Feenstra of Iowa, who lost nominating contests this spring. And two weeks ago, Wyoming Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder and Minnesota businessman and "My Pillow" founder and former CEO Mike Lindell fell short. "There’s no question that an endorsement from President Trump provides a tremendous boost in a Republican primary. But it doesn’t necessarily mean the candidate’s going to win," veteran GOP strategist and communicator Ryan Williams told Fox News Digital. Williams said that "the president still has a firm grip on the party, even in places where a candidate he backed loses a nomination." But he noted that "if there are underlying issues with a candidacy, those can pose problems that even an endorsement can’t overcome." articles.title: Democrat mayor blasted by DHS for 'hunting down' property owners leasing to ICE: 'Unhinged'
articles.summary: DHS calls Boston Mayor Michelle Wu's effort to dissuade property owners from leasing parking to ICE "unhinged," accusing her of hunting them down.
articles.body: The Department of Homeland Security is calling out Boston Democratic Mayor Michelle Wu’s "unhinged" effort to dissuade business owners from leasing to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the city, equating it to "hunting down" private property owners. After Boston banned ICE vehicles from using city-owned parking lots to stage operations, ICE issued a notice seeking to rent hundreds of parking spaces in the city for five years. In response, Wu, an outspoken opponent of President Donald Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda, issued an open letter to parking garage and lot owners throughout Boston in which she revealed the city had submitted a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request "for any local responses to ICE." DHS fired back in an X post, writing that "these actions by sanctuary Mayor Michelle Wu are unhinged." "She knows she has NO authority to block us from using private property. So, she’s hunting down private property owners and threatening them for working with ICE — because she’d rather intimidate law-abiding Bostonians than get criminal illegal aliens OFF the street," wrote DHS. TOM HOMAN FIRES BACK AT FLORIDA DEMOCRAT OVER 'RIDICULOUS' ICE RACIAL PROFILING CLAIM ICE issued a "sources sought" notice last month for "surge parking" in 14 cities across the country. The notice revealed ICE was seeking 249 contiguous parking spaces in Boston. In response, Wu issued an official appeal from the city of Boston for garage and lot owners to "reject ICE staging facilities." She wrote that "were ICE to procure such resources, it would constitute an unprovoked and unwarranted escalation, creating potentially significant risks to public safety and halting economic activity across our entire region." She boasted that she "joined together with six other cities across Greater Boston and signed Executive Orders prohibiting ICE from staging its operations on municipal property and parking lots," adding, "Today, I ask you to join us: Reject any proposition by ICE to facilitate an attack on the people of Boston." Wu also noted that the same day, the city submitted a FOIA request for any local responses to ICE. She told the garage and lot owners, "We will keep you updated as we push for a response," adding, "Thank you again for your partnership." EXCLUSIVE: 5-TIME ILLEGAL ENTRANT ADMITS ‘MISTAKE’ THAT FINALLY GOT HIM BUSTED BY ICE In its FOIA request, which was submitted to ICE and reviewed by Fox News Digital, the city of Boston states that it is seeking "all submissions and/or responses to ICE Sources Sought Notice with Notice ID ‘DHS-ICE-SurgeParking.’" DHS responded to Wu’s FOIA request by calling her a "pro-criminal illegal alien politician" in another X post. The agency said the request also indicates that Wu "admits she has no authority to block ICE from utilizing private property." "If private citizens want to allow federal law enforcement onto their own property, they should be allowed to do so—free of threats, intimidation and coercion from their radical left-wing mayor who shamelessly compared ICE agents to a neo-Nazi group," wrote DHS. Fox News Digital reached out to Wu’s office and the city of Boston for comment. Wu’s FOIA request came after the Boston City Council adopted an "emergency resolution" earlier this month urging the city to "explore all avenues to oppose" proposed parking leases for ICE in downtown Boston. TOM HOMAN EXPLAINS IMMIGRATION STRATEGY FOCUSING ON SANCTUARY CITIES SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The council said that by adopting the emergency resolution, it was calling on the city to "explore available options to prevent the proposed parking leases and expressed its opposition to an increased ICE presence in the city." articles.title: BRUCE PEARL: Conservatives are attacking the very college sports bill that protects women
articles.summary: Retired Auburn coach says critics wrongly claim the Protect College Sports Act guts Title IX, warning that inaction threatens women's and Olympic sports programs.
articles.body: Men don’t belong in women’s sports. That isn’t complicated, but some conservative influencers and interest groups are allowing it to become complicated through careless claims about legislation designed to protect college athletics. I spent nearly five decades coaching college basketball. I know the difference between winning a possession and winning the game. Conservatives now face a similar choice: We can chase applause by attacking allies and mischaracterizing the bill, or we can unite around the facts and win the larger fight for women, fairness and the future of college sports. Some organizations and women’s-sports advocates claim the Protect College Sports Act would "gut" Title IX or invalidate state laws that reserve women’s teams for women. They are wrong. The text says the opposite. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: COLLEGE SPORTS BILL ENTERS LEGISLATIVE 'RED ZONE' AS SEASON KICKS OFF Section 127 explicitly states that nothing in the bill will "override, modify, or amend" Title IX. Female athletes would retain their current legal protections and ability to bring sex-discrimination claims. Section 120 also protects athletes, employees and others from retaliation for reporting discrimination or participating in Title IX proceedings. I spent nearly five decades coaching college basketball. I know the difference between winning a possession and winning the game. Conservatives now face a similar choice: We can chase applause by attacking allies and mischaracterizing the bill, or we can unite around the facts. Critics also claim the bill would erase state laws keeping men out of women’s sports. It would not. The legislation establishes national standards for Division I and Division II competition on limited eligibility questions, including academics, professional status, legal violations, age and years of eligibility. It neither creates a federal right for men to enter women’s competitions nor pre-empts state laws establishing sex-based athletic categories. REPUBLICAN SENATORS FILE AMENDMENT TO STOP COLLEGE SPORTS BILL FROM OVERRIDING STATE WOMEN'S SPORTS LAWS The bill does not expressly create a federal right for biological males to compete in women’s sports, and Section 127 states that nothing in the bill overrides, modifies or amends Title IX. Critics seem to be grasping at anything and eager to disregard the Title IX provisions here. Especially since the Supreme Court ruled in June that schools may keep men out of women’s sports. It also requires governing bodies to enforce rules related to state and federal law and allows individuals to sue when the law is violated. CONGRESS MUST FIX THE PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT BEFORE GIRLS PAY THE PRICE The bill also gives schools a powerful incentive to invest in women’s and Olympic sports. It creates a $22.5 million athlete-retention fund and allows schools to unlock up to an additional $5 million through eligible NIL investments in women’s, Olympic and non-revenue sports. A school seeking the full $27.5 million retention allowance would first need to invest $5 million in those sports. That is an ingenious way to ensure continued investment in programs that might otherwise be left behind. And every year Congress waits, the financial pressure on college athletics grows, and the programs with the fewest resources become even more vulnerable. My 2025 Final Four team had a total NIL budget of approximately $4 million. By the 2027 Final Four, some teams could be operating with budgets approaching $30 million. Conservatives should debate legislation, demand improvements and scrutinize every line. But facts must guide us. Too many Washington organizations would rather score points against perceived rivals than secure lasting victories for women and college athletes. CRUZ AND CANTWELL REFUSE TO BEND TO SEC AND BIG TEN CONCERNS IN REVISED COLLEGE ATHLETICS LEGISLATION Outrage is easy; turning shared principles into law is harder. Infighting only helps the left, which has spent years undermining Title IX while conservatives battle over legislation that expressly preserves it. If we can’t unite and get this done, we will lose college sports as we know them, and women’s and Olympic sports will continue to be among the first casualties. The stakes extend beyond Title IX, and the crisis is no longer theoretical. Thirty-two Division I Olympic-sports programs were cut between the announcement of the House settlement and May 2025. WRAL reported that more than 40 Division I Olympic-sports programs were cut between May 2024 and July 2025, even though 75% of American Olympians in 2024 competed in collegiate athletics. NCAA data Even the University of Arkansas, backed by SEC resources, announced plans to eliminate its tennis programs before donors intervened to save them. If programs at schools like Arkansas are vulnerable, imagine the danger facing smaller schools, women’s teams and non-revenue sports nationwide. Now, those who claim to support the America First movement should get in the game, help Congress finish the job and deliver this win for women and college athletes. Congress now has the opportunity to take important steps to stabilize college sports, support educational opportunities for young women and men, and provide protections for the uniquely American experience of intercollegiate athletics. The Protect College Sports Act is an important step in the right direction, and Congress needs to keep the positive momentum moving forward. Winning the point may feel good. Winning the war matters more.

articles.title: Graham hopes Trump propels her across finish line in South Carolina
articles.summary: The South Carolina Senate runoff on Tuesday is becoming a key test of President Trump’s endorsement power, as he throws all his weight behind a political newcomer seeking to fill shoes left by her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). The race has divided the party between those who back Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.),…
articles.body:
The South Carolina Senate runoff on Tuesday is becoming a key test of President Trump’s endorsement power, as he throws all his weight behind a political newcomer seeking to fill shoes left by her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

The race has divided the party between those who back Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), who was tapped to serve out her brother’s term and whom Trump encouraged to run for another six years, and supporters of Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.), a member of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus with a long history of representing the state.

Trump has leaned into the race in a way he has rarely done this midterm cycle, holding a campaign rally Friday night in Myrtle Beach, S.C., for Graham and attaching his own political clout to the outcome.

“What I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just come and vote. It’s so important,” Trump told supporters at a rally for Graham Friday night in Myrtle Beach.

“So just say that I’m on the ballot one more time,” the president added. “You got to say it, and you got to come out and vote.”

Trump’s MAGA Inc. also spent over $827,000 for Graham, marking the super PAC’s first independent expenditure since March.

Graham’s support has come from establishment Republicans , including the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the president himself , political action committees and business executives. The Palmetto State’s governor, who appointed Graham to her brother’s seat , is campaigning with the senator on Monday.

Norman, meanwhile, has self-funded much of his campaign and has leaned on his conservative policy chops, while accusing Graham of being “controlled by the Washington elite.”

But with such a short campaign window and a limited public record to run on, every move Graham has made matters.

So during last week’s debate, when Graham struggled to answer a rudimentary question on foreign policy — a subject matter that came to define much of her late brother’s legacy in public service — the moment came to dominate the news cycle.

“That’s the kind of thing that, if she does lose on Tuesday, I feel like we’ll be chalking entirely up to that,” Geoffrey Skelley, Decision Desk HQ’s chief elections analyst, said of the debate flub.

“Of course that would be simplistic, but if you’re not familiar, and you find yourself as the front-runner … that really stands out as a defining moment for your candidacy,” he continued. “You can see how she might end up blowing this.”

Norman has pledged not to go negative on the campaign against Graham, saying last week, “She’s been through a lot. … She really has, losing a brother. I’m not going to do that,” referring to his decision not to run antagonistic ads.

But the congressman has still highlighted Graham’s lack of political experience, both on the debate stage and in the days that followed.

“By her choice, she’s running for the United States Senate. It’s a six-year term,” Norman said during the debate. “You need to get fully versed in what issues you’re going to be dealing with. This isn’t a get-training-on-the-job. You can’t do that.”

At last week’s debate, Graham responded that she was “not that informed on national security” when asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues.

Graham then touted her family’s service in the military, saying she’s “not a polished politician up here. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military.”

In an interview with Fox News’s Sean Hannity the following evening, Graham acknowledged the fumble and leaned into attacks on her lack of experience, saying she’s since talked to voters and they appreciate her candor and that she’s not a “career politician.”

“I tripped up on one question last night regarding Taiwan, but you know, I’ve said many times, I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician,” she said. “I was just honest, and I think that’s kind of a foreign concept.”

Trump echoed a similar defense when asked Friday about the gaffe, telling reporters that Graham “was being honest.”

“She’s surrounded by very good people, and she said that she’s totally for the military,” the president said.

As Graham has continued to brand herself as a political outsider, her opponent has repeatedly attacked her as the candidate backed by “the Washington elite,” pointing to her donors, which include Boeing’s political action committee, private equity firm Blackstone’s chief executive officer, social media platform TikTok’s head of public policy, and tech company Palantir’s head of defense chief of staff, according to South Carolina-based news outlet The State .

But Graham has pushed back on these efforts, saying earlier this month, according to The State, “When people give to me, that means they support me.”

“That doesn’t necessarily mean I support them,” she added.

The race has drawn millions of dollars from individual donors as well as from super PACs. In the last week of the race alone, Security is Strength PAC contributed more than $1.8 million and Palmetto Action gave nearly $1.2 million to boost Graham or oppose Norman, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) records. Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, a renewable energy-backed group, announced on Aug. 14 that it would spend $1 million to defeat Norman.

Norman’s funding from outside groups is dwarfed by Graham’s, but his campaign has benefited from his personal wealth. He donated $1.3 million to his own campaign on Aug. 17, four days after giving another $400,000, according to FEC reports.

Endorsements in the race have also swung more in Graham’s favor. On Monday alone, South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster (R) campaigned with the senator, and Trump joined a tele-rally with Graham at night for a last-ditch push to encourage South Carolinians to vote.

But last Friday, Norman got a boost when former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford (R), who came in fourth place during the special primary this month, backed Norman over Graham.

Rep. Russell Fry (R-S.C.), who came in a close third, backed Graham, who rallied in his district with Trump on Friday.

The results of the Aug. 11 primary were close, with Graham and Norman advancing with 32.75 percent and 24.62 percent, respectively, followed by Fry with 19.66 percent and Sanford with 14.94 percent.

Public polling has been limited in the couple of weeks since, and the dynamics have changed. As a result, many political observers are going in blind on Tuesday, waiting to see to what extent the debate, cash and Trump’s support will make a difference in the outcome.

“If you’re in the lead and … you have the support of the president, it’s a pretty good place to be,” Skelley said. “So I’m not necessarily saying that I think Graham is going to lose. I just think that this race really does feel up in the air.”

articles.title: Trump’s fight with GOP senators over trade intensifies
articles.summary: President Trump is headed for a clash with Senate Republicans over his decision to pause tariffs on beef imports while ratcheting up tariffs on key Canadian goods. Trump’s plan to exempt 300,000 tons of product for ground beef from out-of-quota tariffs to address Americans’ concerns about high food prices while simultaneously threatening Canada with 50…
articles.body:
President Trump is headed for a clash with Senate Republicans over his decision to pause tariffs on beef imports while ratcheting up tariffs on key Canadian goods .

Trump’s plan to exempt 300,000 tons of product for ground beef from out-of-quota tariffs to address Americans’ concerns about high food prices while simultaneously threatening Canada with 50 percent tariffs on imports that could impact auto and housing prices has sparked a furious response from GOP senators across the party’s political spectrum.

“I think it’s a mistake. It’s what happens when he has advisers trying to micromanage things. They’re skating where the puck is versus where it needs to be. If you think that providing subsidized beef for some period of time is going to make farmers happy and prices go down on systemic basis, you’re wrong. It doesn’t happen,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said at the Capitol Monday.

“Every time the government micromanages the economy, consumers suffer,” Tillis warned.

Tillis is one of several Republicans from an agriculture-heavy state to warn against allowing cheap beef imports to flood the U.S. market over the next three months — something that Trump hopes will bring down the price of an American diet staple through the midterm election.

Senate Republican Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.), the second-ranking member of the Senate Republican leadership, declared Monday that “Americans want US beef on the table — not foreign imports.”

“Wyoming ranchers produce the highest quality beef in the world. Our ranchers don’t ask for special treatment. They simply want a fair marketplace. It needs to be easier – not harder – for Wyoming ranchers to feed America,” he posted on X, the social media platform.

Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), the third-ranking member of the Senate GOP leadership, warned that opening U.S. markets to cheaper imports is “ill-advised” and will hurt domestic producers.

“Beef prices are too high for a simple reason: Our cattle herd is too small. Imported beef below market prices will only put more pressure on our cattlemen,” Cotton argued on social media.

“I have advised the President against this ill-advised action in the past and I now urge him to reconsider. We need to support our cattlemen, grow the herd, and let the market work,” Cotton wrote.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) also took to social media to dismiss Trump’s move as a “quick fix” and argued it’s out of step with the president’s efforts to rebuild domestic manufacturing capacity with tariffs, such as those he’s threatening against Canada.

“What our market really needs is a stable, America-First national policy that promotes American beef rather than continuing to import foreign beef as a quick ‘fix.’ This instability harms hardworking American ranchers and consumers who want American-made beef,” he wrote.

“This is the exact opposite approach we take compared to manufacturing, and it doesn’t make sense,” Rounds added.

Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.), a member of the Agriculture Committee, shared that relatively strong beef prices were a “bright spot” for the nation’s “struggling agriculture industry.”

“Importing beef below market prices will only put further downward pressure on the livestock sector, endangering what has been a bright spot in a struggling agriculture industry,” the Kansas senator wrote on social media. “I urge President Trump to halt this action, listen to ranchers and let the free markets work.”

Republican Sens. Chuck Grassley (Iowa), Deb Fischer (Neb.) and Pete Ricketts (Neb.) also raised alarms over foreign beef showing up in American grocery stores.

Grassley said he was “concerned” while Fischer said she was “extremely disappointed by this decision” and Ricketts warned that “flooding the market with lower quality beef” would hurt Nebraska farmers and ranchers.

Yet Trump appears to be more sensitive to ground beef prices, which have risen by approximately 20 percent since he took office in January of 2025.

The average price of ground beef reached $6.89 per pound in July.

Trump pledged that imported beef will be sold at “25 percent below current market prices” over the next three months.

Some Democratic candidates, such as Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek who’s eyeing a Senate seat, are highlighting “skyrocketing” beef prices on the campaign trail.

But many Republicans don’t think that allowing cheap imports into the country is the best solution.

“Increasing beef imports would lead to more uncertainty and instability for our farmers,” said Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), the GOP candidate in Iowa’s Senate race.

“We should be focused on cutting red tape for cattle producers, lowering the cost of production and supporting market-based solutions to support Iowa producers and lower costs for consumers,” she wrote on social media.

The criticism from GOP senators of Trump’s decision to pause tariffs on beef imports comes as other Republican senators are pushing back against Trump’s 50 percent tariffs on an array of Canadian imports and his threat to impose equally high fees on even more.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who faces a tough reelection race in a state that voted for former President Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris in the last two presidential elections, called Trump’s threatened tariffs against Canada “a mistake.”

“We produce a lot in Maine — our blueberries, our potatoes, our lobster, our lumber — that is processed across the border. If it comes back with a huge tariff on it, perhaps as much as 50 percent, that increases the cost of eating, building homes and merch[andising] our best-known products,” Collins told News Center Maine in an interview Monday.

Collins was one of four Republicans who voted last year to revoke Trump’s tariffs against Canada. She and Republican Sens. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), Rand Paul (Ky.) and Mitch McConnell (Ky.) voted with Democrats to pass a resolution blocking them.

Six House Republicans voted with Democrats to pass a similar measure in the House last year.

Former Trump economic adviser Stephen Moore warned that any gains that domestic businesses might get from higher tariffs on Canadian goods are likely outweighed by the “pain” felt by U.S. consumers and businesses that import Canadian products or sell to Canadian markets.

“Probably the pain is not worth the gain. And you know, I’ve been a bit of a skeptic on the tariff front with respect to the Trump strategy,” Moore told Fox Business in an interview Monday.

He warned that raising the cost of Canadian goods may come while Americans are still coping with higher energy prices because of Iran war’s impact on oil and gas prices.

“We’re in a sticky situation obviously in Iran with respect to those negotiations. Now … do I think now is a good time to fight a trade war with Canada? Probably not,” he said. “Commodity prices are rising right now in the U.S. That’s a bad sign. That’s an indication that inflation continues to tick up.”

Tillis on Monday warned that charging steep tariffs on Canadian goods threatens to disrupt the economies of border states — such as Maine — that are closely integrated with the Canadian economy.

“Let the economy do what the economy’s doing. Get the trade relationships with Canada done versus all this volatility. You’re going to address more price fluctuations by doing this than all these gimmicks,” Tillis said.

The North Carolina senator warned that Republicans are running out of time to help farmers before the midterm elections as both a farm bill, which includes relief programs for ranchers hurt by drought and fire, and a budget reconciliation package, which includes $12 billion in emergency assistance to farmers, is stalled in the Senate.

“We’ve got 71 days” until the election “and right now we don’t have a positive message to tell farm country,” he said. “And we haven’t since Liberation Day last year, which is why I was concerned.”

Trump announced sweeping global tariffs on April 2, 2025, which the president proclaimed “Liberation Day.”

articles.title: The Memo: Trump and Bessent crank up economic pressure on Iran as other options fall short
articles.summary: Six months into the war on Iran — and with less than three months left before the midterms — the Trump administration has decided it’s time for Plan C. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out his ambitions for an “economic onslaught” against the Islamic Republic that would target its “financial connections around the…
articles.body:
Six months into the war on Iran — and with less than three months left before the midterms — the Trump administration has decided it’s time for Plan C.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out his ambitions for an “economic onslaught” against the Islamic Republic that would target its “financial connections around the globe.”

The hope within the administration seems to be that turning up the economic heat on Iran can produce tangible results without the baleful complications that could result from the two other broad options before the president.

If President Trump were to return to all-out war, he would risk a new spike in oil prices, Iranian reprisals aimed at U.S. allies in the Gulf, and a further diminution of American munition stockpiles. Even then, it is not clear that a definitive victory would be achieved without putting U.S. boots on Iranian soil — a scenario that has vanishingly thin support from the public.

If, on the other hand, Trump were to sue for peace right now, Iranian recalcitrance — and an apparent belief in Tehran that they retain plenty of leverage — would require him to make sizeable concessions.

The memorandum of understanding signed in June provided a preview of how such an approach would be received: Negatively.

The memorandum drew criticism from GOP hawks, who suggested it was too soft on Iran; from liberal opponents, who asked rhetorically what the war had been for in the first place; and from Israel, which jointly launched the war with the U.S. in late February.

So, on Monday it fell to Bessent to put some flesh on the bones of Trump’s earlier threats to up the economic pressure on Iran. The president, in a morning social media post, had insisted in his customary all-caps style that “IRAN IS COMPLETELY COLLAPSING!!!”

The Treasury secretary communicates in a different register to his boss, but his language was aggressive all the same.

The administration’s objective, he said, was “to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”

Taking questions from reporters after his prepared remarks, Bessent characterized the U.S. as intent upon the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran.

When it came to the U.S. desire to see other nations comply with Washington’s demands to cut off Iran or face secondary sanctions, Bessent warned, “We do not have infinite patience here.”

There were some definite lines of economic attack — but also a lot of detail that was not filled in.

For example, Bessent asserted that five areas of activity by which Iran sustains itself would be targeted: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. He also insisted that branches of Iran’s Bank Melli “must be shuttered and dark.”

Bessent also contended, even as he spoke, that an office within the Treasury Department was “sanctioning over 60 entities, individuals and vessels around the world that enable the Iranian regime to procure illicit nuclear and missile technology, conduct cyber operations and generate oil revenue.”

Yet, alongside the tough talk, there was also some vagueness.

Importantly, a sizeable question mark hangs over how aggressive the administration is prepared to be with China, which is by far the largest buyer of Iranian oil exports.

Asked about that topic, Bessent asserted both that “no one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions” and that “the best way to engage with countries is through quiet diplomacy.”

It is, of course, rather debatable how committed the Trump administration is to quiet diplomacy. A few hours before Bessent’s appearance before the cameras, Trump had delivered a new jab in an unrelated trade dispute with the U.S.’s northern neighbor, beginning a lengthy social media post by declaring, “Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years.”

That being so, Bessent’s supposed commitment to a softer, more private approach could also function to provide cover for ambivalence about how hard to push Beijing.

The unignorable backdrop to all the machinations is the unpopularity of the war with the American public.

Trump’s approval on Iran in the RealClearPolitics polling average is deep underwater. Roughly 61 percent of Americans disapprove of his handling of the issue, while about 35 percent approve.

The war is intertwined with voters’ chief concern — rising prices and the cost of living. The average gas price nationally was roughly $4.10 per gallon on Monday, according to AAA , having been just below $3 before the war began.

Inflationary pressures, in part caused by the Iran war, are also part of the reason why there have been some jitters on the bond market recently. Bessent stepped in to try to calm the unease last week, with only partial success.

Put it all together, and it is an inhospitable landscape for Republicans seeking office in November’s midterms.

For now, the administration is clearly recalibrating its rhetoric.

Even the pugilistic Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters on Monday that, although he was not “foreclosing” using direct strikes on Iran, “economic pressure, we know, hurts them the most right now .”

Bessent, in a lesser-noted part of his Monday remarks, characterized the U.S. armed forces as having “laid the groundwork” for the achievement of American objectives.

This was a notably more circumspect assessment than those given by other senior administration officials in the early part of the war.

So, for now, the Iranian economy is the battlefield.

The big question is how fast, if at all, the U.S. can secure a meaningful victory.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: South Carolina runoff pits America First against MAGA
articles.summary: Voters, especially Republican primary voters, don’t tend to make their decisions based on what’s going on overseas. But with Uncle Sam’s place in the world looking a little unsteady and a doozy of a debate gaffe in a snap election, we suddenly have in today’s South Carolina Senate runoff the first big electoral test of…
articles.body:
Voters, especially Republican primary voters, don’t tend to make their decisions based on what’s going on overseas.

But with Uncle Sam’s place in the world looking a little unsteady and a doozy of a debate gaffe in a snap election, we suddenly have in today’s South Carolina Senate runoff the first big electoral test of President Trump’s Iran war strategy with Republican voters.

Sen. Darline Graham’s (R-S.C.) already-legendary line — “I’m not that informed on national security” — is thought by many to have recast what had appeared to be a perfunctory runoff with Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) into a competitive race. I say perfunctory because in the first round, the MAGA candidates got most of the vote, almost all of which presumably would filter down to Graham in today’s contest.

There were five candidates who got at least 5 percent of the vote in the first round of the snap primary on Aug. 11, held to replace Graham’s brother, Lindsey. The elder Graham died in July after winning renomination for a fifth Senate term, leaving the state GOP without a Senate candidate in a good Democratic year — one in which the blue team happens to have a nonterrible Senate nominee in Annie Andrews. It’s South Carolina, where no Democratic Senate candidate has come within even 10 points of winning in decades. But still, a bad enough Republican nominee in a bad enough year could have put the Palmetto State race on the map, at least notionally.

There’s plenty that’s weird and wild in South Carolina Republican politics, so Gov. Henry McMaster (R) took no chances and appointed Darline Graham to serve out the final months of her brother’s term. That appointment and her decision to seek a full, six-year term came at the behest of Trump, who has had his own troubles with South Carolina politics.

Before Lindsey Graham became Trump’s wingman and shadow secretary of State, he had been among Trump’s fiercest early critics. And then there’s former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley (R), who went the other direction, serving deferentially as Trump’s first-term ambassador to the United Nations before running a dogged if doomed race against Trump as he sought renomination in 2024. Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) also opposed Trump that year, but only halfheartedly and not for very long.

Knowing that South Carolina can be problematic and looking for another member of the Senate MAGA caucus, Trump clearly judged that backing a sentimental favorite in the beloved sister of the late senator would be easy electoral politics and give him an easy vote in Washington, where things have only been getting harder for the lame-duck commander in chief.

In that way, Graham’s gaffe was proof of concept for Trump. Asked about her professed ignorance ahead of his trip to campaign for Graham, Trump told reporters , “She is going to do what the military wants, and really what the president wants. She understands that national security is my thing.” That presumably applies when his “thing” is increasingly unpopular with voters.

Trump’s electoral assumption about Graham was proven right in Round 1 of the snap primary, when she got about a third of the vote, besting Norman by 8 points. Norman is not MAGA but rather a dissident from South Carolina’s underlying don’t-tread-on-me tradition. The House Freedom Caucus is pretty much a MAGA operation now, but back when Norman joined in 2017, there was still a little of the rebellious streak left. Norman has always had a little of Marjorie Taylor Greene energy about him — more about the movement than the man. But he’s also won friends among traditional conservatives for his hawkishness on spending and Reaganite foreign policy. It wasn’t just home-state sentiment that led Norman to back Haley in 2024 or Haley to back him now.

In third place on Aug. 11 was Rep. Russell Fry (R-S.C.), who is stone-cold MAGA to his core. Team Trump backed Fry in his 2022 primary bid against then-Rep. Tom Rice (R-S.C.), an old-school conservative who had voted to impeach Trump for trying to overturn the 2020 election. Fry beat Rice in a major show of strength for Trump early in his interregnum, making Fry a made man in MAGA. He got nearly 20 percent of the vote in Round 1 and then, to the surprise of no one, fell in behind Trump-endorsed Graham for the runoff.

Next in the running was Mark Sanford, the former governor and congressman who was a conservative heartthrob until the vivid unraveling of his marriage while still the state’s chief executive. Sanford is neither MAGA nor America First in any strict sense. He’s a traditional, small-government conservative with some areas of overlap with both groups but is clearly and stubbornly a dissident. He is also a hated figure in MAGA World for his frequent opposition to Trump during Sanford’s House tenure. No surprise, then, that he is backing Norman over Graham on Tuesday. It’s an echo of the onetime conservative dream team in the state that once included Sanford, Haley, Scott and former Rep. Trey Gowdy (R-S.C.), now long eclipsed by Trump and McMaster’s very effective machine.

Rounding out the top five was Mark Lynch, who has a massive appliance store in South Carolina’s Upstate. Lynch proved that he is more America First than MAGA when he ran against Lindsey Graham in the original June primary. While Lynch is part of a movement that takes out-there stances on things like allegations of election corruption and vaccines , he is willing to publicly disagree with Trump. And given that his central charge against the elder Graham was that he was too much of an internationalist, one suspects Lynch isn’t a “forever war” kind of guy. He too has endorsed Norman .

All of which makes the Iran question particularly interesting. Darline Graham accidentally summed up the MAGA Iran position: Back the president and let him do his “thing.” The America First position tends to be that the war was a betrayal of Trump’s promises and a mistake from the start that is only getting worse. The conservative stance seems to be that bombing Iran could have been the right move but that Trump has subsequently blundered it away. The candidates in this race have been cagy about their own stances, but voters are going to make their own inferences.

Not everyone who voted in Round 1 will vote in Round 2, but we can use the results as a rough guide for where today’s electorate started. The MAGA candidates — Graham and Fry — combined for 52 percent of the vote. America Firsters and conservatives — Norman, Sanford and Lynch — combined for 46 percent, with 2 percent sprinkled across minor candidates.

The question today is whether Graham’s textbook Kinsley gaffe is worth at least 4 points for Norman with swing among voters who are having their own doubts about whether the president should be running foreign policy without supervision. Norman’s hope has got to be that he’s got enough cred with both America First and the conservatives to make it happen.

Stirewalt is the politics editor for The Hill, veteran campaign and elections journalist and best-selling author of books about American political history.

articles.title: Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932. Will that change in November?
articles.summary: Adam Hamilton, a liberal megachurch pastor, is challenging incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall in this year’s midterm election
articles.body:
In one of the first ads of his campaign to represent Kansas in the US Senate, the Democrat Adam Hamilton stands grilling steaks at a barbecue and attacks his opponent, Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican, for supporting "tariffs and war".

If history is any guide, it is Hamilton who is set to get cooked. Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and more than half a century has passed since one of their nominees even came close. But he and his supporters believe circumstances have conspired to end this streak – and potentially deliver Democrats control of the Senate.

"When it comes to tariffs, healthcare, immigration, when it comes to the war in Iran, these are all things that are having a negative impact on people in Kansas," Hamilton, 62, said in an interview. "That makes this a particularly vulnerable time for Roger Marshall. Then, I think I'm a particularly strong candidate. I wouldn't have got in the race if I didn't."

The founder of the largest Methodist denomination in the US, Hamilton won 35% of the vote in the 11-candidate Democratic primary earlier this month. His campaign recently announced he had broken a quarterly fundraising record in the state, and two major election forecasters say the Senate race has grown more competitive since Hamilton won his party's primary, though Marshall is still favored to win.

For national Democratic leaders, the possibility of a close Senate race in Kansas is enticing. Their path to retaking Congress's upper chamber involves winning at least three seats in states that Donald Trump carried two years ago, and they've named Alaska, North Carolina, Ohio, Texas and Iowa as among their best bets to do so.

The US president's slumping approval ratings and the Iran war's impact on prices for gasoline and other staples are seen as boosting Democrats' chances in those states, but Kansas is a bit redder. Trump carried it two years ago by a 16 percentage point margin.

This week, Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer told Punchbowl News that if the November elections wind up producing a "blue wave" of Democratic victories, Hamilton may well win.

Asked what he thought of Schumer's prediction, Hamilton said: "I don't agree with that. I think there will be a blue wave, but I'm telling you, here in Kansas, we have a real chance to win. I don't care what else happens across the country."

No Kansas Democrat has won a full term in the US Senate since attorney George McGill in 1932, the longest streak of any state. In 1974, Senator Bob Dole, who would go on to become the chamber's Republican leader and run unsuccessfully against President Bill Clinton in 1996, nearly lost his bid for a second term, but Republicans have wiped out their opponents ever since.

Democrats and their causes have had better luck at the state level. The governor's mansion has seesawed between the two parties since the late 1950s, and the race this year to replace outgoing Democratic governor Laura Kelly is viewed as a toss-up. After the supreme court overturned Roe v Wade, Kansans have on two occasions rejected Republican-backed attempts to curb abortion access in the state.

"Kansas voters, the majority anyway, there's something about the Senate where, especially those moderate Republicans, still won't pull the trigger in terms of enough of them voting for a Democrat, where they will for governor," said Bob Beatty, a longtime state politics watcher who chairs the political science department at Washburn University in Topeka.

But Hamilton's experience in leading a church gives him a unique skill set that Beatty predicts will make for "a very competitive race" against Marshall. "What Hamilton has going for him is the communication side. He's been giving sermons, AKA speeches, to crowds of thousands for years," he said.

Marshall is an OB/GYN who represented western Kansas in the US House of Representatives, then won election to the Senate in 2020 and embraced Trump's debunked claims of fraud in that year's presidential vote. He has been an ally of Trump in Congress, and last year left a town hall early after attendees pressed him about the Trump administration's funding cuts and layoffs of federal employees. A spokesperson for the senator did not respond to a request for comment.

Hamilton said he decided to jump into the Senate race ahead of Easter, as he prepared to preach the sermon on the mount at his Church of the Resurrection outside Kansas City, which boasts around 24,000 congregants. He mulled running as an independent, but ultimately filed as a Democrat, saying he was concerned that he'd split the vote if he wasn't in a party and agreed with its views on "healthcare, education [and] social safety nets".

"Those are things that matter a lot to me, and my faith leads in that direction," he said.

A self-described "moderate or independent-minded Democrat", his campaign recently released an ad where Hamilton likens Kansas's position in the middle of the country to his own approach to the politics that would await him in Washington DC.

Hamilton has criticized Marshall for being "a spokesperson for Washington and Donald Trump instead of representing the people of Kansas", and accused the senator of spending most of his time in Florida. Marshall has acknowledged owning a property in that state, but recently told reporters it was destroyed by a hurricane. Earlier this month, the Topeka Capital-Journal reported he'd put the Sarasota property on the market for $1.45m.

The senator recently called his opponent a "megachurch pastor that's too woke for Kansas", the Capital-Journal reported. Main Street Fund, a Massachusetts-based Super Pac that lists its treasurer a consultant who has worked for Republican campaigns, spent more than $600,000 this month to air ads in Kansas, making a similar accusation against Hamilton that the Kansas City Star found relied on snippets from his sermons that were taken out of context.

Like so much in his career, Hamilton's chances may come down to faith. Jim Slattery, a Democratic former congressman from the state who supports Hamilton, described him as "a known quantity in the Methodist world in Kansas" and among Christians in the Kansas City area who may win if he gains the support of right-leaning Catholic voters opposed to the war with Iran.

"The reason Hamilton is a compelling candidate is because he can, and he has the ability to, dramatically expand the audience for a Democrat candidate in Kansas," Slattery said. "It's the bottom line."
