articles.title: Smithsonian-linked museum in El-Sayed’s backyard puts America’s post-9/11 response on trial
articles.summary: A Smithsonian Institution affiliate in Dearborn features exhibits arguing Arabs suffered unfair treatment after the Sept. 11 attacks on America.
articles.body: DEARBORN, MI – Nearly 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks, a Smithsonian affiliate in Michigan continues to use its 9/11 exhibits and anniversary programming to focus on discrimination and government actions in the attacks' aftermath, while giving less attention to the nearly 3,000 people killed that day, Fox News Digital found. The Arab American National Museum in Dearborn, Michigan, features an exhibit arguing that Arab Americans "suffered two-fold as a result of the tragic events of September 11th," both from the attacks themselves and from what the museum describes as unfair treatment by the U.S. government afterward. Since its founding, the museum has repeatedly hosted programs examining what it describes as discriminatory consequences of the U.S. response to 9/11. Fox News Digital visited the museum earlier this month, reviewed its exhibits and gift shop, and examined years of anniversary programming and federal funding records. The AANM has received hundreds of thousands of dollars in grant funding from the National Endowment for the Humanities and is also an affiliate of the Smithsonian Institution. The Smithsonian has been under intense scrutiny from conservative lawmakers in recent months for allegedly allowing political bias to influence its presentation of history. TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED One placard criticizes the government’s post-9/11 detention of immigrants investigated for possible terrorist links, noting that "virtually none were charged" in connection with terrorism. "The Arab American community suffered two-fold as a result of the tragic events of September 11th. As with all Americans, they suffered the horror and grief. However, Arab Americans were unfairly held responsible, yet not a single Arab American was found guilty of any connection to September 11th," it reads. On Sept. 11, 2001, 19 al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four passenger planes, crashing two into the World Trade Center, and one into the Pentagon. Passengers and crew fought back aboard United Flight 93, the fourth plane, prompting the hijackers to crash the plane in Pennsylvania. The attacks killed 2,977 people and triggered the largest investigation in FBI history. The museum placard also argues that Arabs faced harsher immigration enforcement after the attacks, saying some were "deported for minor visa violations or petty offenses which previously would have been overlooked." HISTORIAN BLASTS SMITHSONIAN'S ACTIVISM SHIFT AFTER FIRST VISIT IN OVER A DECADE: 'COMPLETELY DIFFERENT PLACE' In the 11 months after the attacks, immigration authorities detained 762 noncitizens on immigration charges in connection with the FBI’s terrorism investigation, including for overstaying visas or entering the country illegally, according to a Justice Department inspector general report. The watchdog found that some detainees with no terrorism ties were treated harshly and held under unnecessarily restrictive conditions. Public opinion also showed a more complicated picture of the post-9/11 backlash. President George W. Bush publicly urged Americans not to blame Muslims for the attacks, and polling later suggested attitudes toward Muslim Americans actually improved in the immediate aftermath. The share of Americans who viewed Muslim Americans favorably rose from 45% in March 2001 to 59% in November, two months after the attacks, according to the Pew Research Center. Beyond its permanent exhibit, AANM has repeatedly used programming around the 9/11 anniversary to examine discrimination and law-enforcement policies affecting Arab and Muslim communities. The museum holds a "solidarity" town hall each year, where criticism of the American reaction to 9/11 is often the focus. The online description of the event does not mention the deaths connected to the attacks themselves, but rather "offers a safe space for communities to reflect and engage in dialogue about the harmful prejudices that Arab and Muslim (and anyone perceived to be Arab or Muslim) individuals face on both an individual and systemic level." One such town hall in 2018 examined "how communities of color have been targeted through the frame of national security and profiled as violent threats." A year later, the AANM’s annual town, which received support from the National Endowment for the Arts, criticized how "institutions and communities of color have been infiltrated" by law enforcement as well as how leaders of those groups have been "targeted" following 9/11. SMITHSONIAN AMERICA 250 EXHIBIT FEATURES 3X MORE LIBERAL ITEMS THAN CONSERVATIVE ONES The AANM was founded in 2005, partially in response to the increased scrutiny directed at the Arab American community following the attack on the World Trade Center. In addition to receiving well over half a million dollars in funding from the NEH over its lifetime to support its exhibits and educational programming, the museum also benefited from a $385,000 grant from the Department of Housing and Urban Development which helped it expand its physical footprint in 2013. It received further HUD funding, over half a million dollars, between 2017 and 2019 as well as at least $50,000 from the State Department between 2016 and 2017, according to annual reports published by the museum. Dearborn, where about 54.5% of residents are of Middle Eastern or North African descent, is a key political center in Michigan ahead of one of the country’s most competitive Senate races this year. Socialist-aligned Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for the Senate, drew strong support from the city earlier this month. The museum’s focus extends beyond its criticism of the U.S. response to 9/11. On Sept. 10 — the eve of the 25th anniversary of the attacks — the AANM is scheduled to host a screening of "Seeds for Liberation," a film that portrays Hamas’ Oct. 7 terrorist attack as part of a decades-long Palestinian "struggle" and places it within a broader history of "anti-imperialist and decolonial movements." During Fox News Digital’s visit earlier this month, a section of the museum was dedicated to art criticizing Israel's alleged "occupation" of Palestinian land. One piece of art, the word "wall" presented in a stylized print, accuses the Israeli government of perpetuating a system of "apartheid." The art installation broadly accuses Israel of targeting civilians in military operations, denying basic necessities to Palestinians and unjustly occupying land. FORMER DEMOCRATIC STAFFERS, DEI LEADERS SHAPE SMITHSONIAN LEADERSHIP AMID POLITICAL FIRESTORM One placard accompanying a sculpture states that Israel has killed more than 2,000 Palestinian children since Sept. 29, 2000, citing If Americans Knew (IAK). The placard’s sourcing is itself controversial. Some pro-Palestinian organizations have distanced themselves from IAK over allegations of antisemitism and ties to white supremacists, allegations the group has disputed. IAK also operates a news site that has published articles rejecting the designation of Hamas as a terrorist organization. Another placard attached to a sculpture pulls a quote from Defense of Children International Palestine, which the Israeli government designated as a terrorist organization in 2021. DCIP and human rights groups have disputed the designation. The museum gift shop also sells Palestinian-themed merchandise, including map-shaped magnets and key chains, coloring books promising to help children "explore Palestinian heritage" and keffiyehs. IN CHARTS: A VISUAL BREAKDOWN OF THE SMITHSONIAN'S BILLION-DOLLAR TAXPAYER-FUNDED BUDGET CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The AANM, Smithsonian, NEA and NEH did not respond to requests for comment after being reached by Fox News Digital on Friday. Smithsonian affiliates, like the AANM, are independently operated museums that maintain formal partnerships with the Smithsonian, providing them with access to artifact loans, educational resources and consultations from institutional experts. In recent months, the Smithsonian has faced mounting pressure from Republican lawmakers and the president over allegations that its museums advance left-of-center ideological causes through their exhibits. Officials have threatened funding cuts against the institution if it does not root out what the Trump administration characterizes as anti-American bias.

articles.title: Florida, hard-hit by Obamacare drop-off, feels the squeeze of rising healthcare costs
articles.summary: Florida chef Elijah Button was chopping onions in June when his knife slipped and sliced his middle finger to the bone.  After Republicans in Congress let en...
articles.body:
ST. CLOUD, Fla. (AP) — Florida chef Elijah Button was chopping onions in June when his knife slipped and sliced his middle finger to the bone.

It was his worst kitchen accident to date. But having given up his Affordable Care Act health insurance plan in January because of a $100 monthly premium hike he couldn't afford, the 21-year-old in St. Cloud didn't have the money for emergency care.

"Going to the hospital for it wasn't even an option," he said, gesturing toward his finger before preparing a pot roast for his aunt and uncle in their suburban home. "My first thought was, 'how am I going to fix this?'"

After Republicans in Congress let enhanced federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act health plans expire in January, millions of Americans including Button had to decide whether to keep insurance that often doubled or tripled in cost — or risk going without it.

Months later, with no action from lawmakers to replace the lost funds, they're facing the consequences. Some are dealing with strained budgets and exorbitant medical bills, while others avoid the doctor in fear of the cost.

Florida, whose large population of gig workers, entrepreneurs and small business owners relies heavily on the federal health insurance marketplace, has become one of the nation's most visible epicenters of that impact.

Figures first reported by The Associated Press showed that about 440,000 Floridians dropped their Affordable Care Act plans this year — more than in any other state . Thousands more who kept coverage are struggling to get by, as prices of necessities like groceries and gasoline remain steep, and health insurers project another year of double-digit premium hikes .

While Florida had the most affected residents, its struggles are reflective of broader nationwide concerns over rising healthcare costs and a lack of meaningful policy to address them.

In the deep-red state where congressional districts were recently redrawn to strongly favor Republicans, the cost of healthcare is a major campaign issue. Republican midterm candidates have been promoting fraud crackdowns to protect federal health programs, while Democrats have been urging voters to help Congress change hands so they can restore subsidies.

Button, who is estranged from his parents, asked his uncle for help with his bloodied finger. With a butterfly bandage, splint and daily cleanings and dressings, it healed. But the scar still gnaws at Button as a symbol of what else could go wrong.

"It just feels like I'm living in a house of cards," he said.

Florida's population and politics make it ground zero for ACA fallout

Last fall, debate over the expiring subsidies consumed Congress, resulting in a record 43-day government shutdown as Democrats insisted on extending the COVID-era assistance and most Republicans refused.

Fast forward almost a year and lawmakers rarely reference the topic anymore. The administration says it is addressing affordability with fraud-busting efforts and deals with drug companies, but Congress hasn't passed any significant legislation to lower health costs.

In part due to its large number of construction, hospitality and small business workers — and also because its Republican-led legislature never expanded the Medicaid safety-net health program — Florida has the largest Affordable Care Act enrollment in the country. At just over 3.8 million enrollees, it represents about a fifth of the nation's total enrolled population.

Of the roughly 443,000 Floridians who left the marketplace, most are likely going without insurance, according to Cynthia Cox, a vice president at the healthcare research nonprofit KFF. She said that's because it is typically a "place of last resort" to get coverage.

The data doesn't tell the stories of those who kept insurance. Tracy Rand, a licensed mental health counselor in Leesburg, Florida, is one of them.

Ever since getting her ovaries removed last year due to benign but painful tumors, she has had severe menopause symptoms that require medication, including an overactive bladder and hot flashes that cause piercing headaches.

She uses clear plastic containers to organize the more than 30 medicines and supplements she takes daily, their bottles crammed into a living-room drawer and a tray on her kitchen counter.

The 51-year-old's Affordable Care Act plan was going to surge in price this year from $55 a month to $1,100 a month, so she downgraded. Her new plan, with higher deductibles and copays, costs $160 a month.

To make that work in her budget, Rand quit a doctoral program she was working toward, started buying groceries at cheaper stores, gave up once-monthly dinners out with her husband and stopped meeting friends regularly at a paint-your-own pottery studio.

It's been a difficult adjustment, but a necessary one for her health.

Rand said the prospect of insurers raising rates again fills her with dread.

"I don't know what else we can get rid of," she said, covering her face with her hands. "I don't know if we're going to have to file bankruptcy.″

Clinics for the uninsured are a saving grace — but they can't take everyone

In Orlando's leafy, brick-paved neighborhood of Colonialtown South, Tarsha Watson found her lifeline. A clinic there called Grace Medical Home provides low-income, uninsured Floridians with comprehensive care for a $5 per-visit fee.

Watson, 54, has a master's degree in business administration, but she hasn't been able to find work since losing her job two years ago. That means she doesn't have health insurance. When she explored Affordable Care Act coverage, she was quoted $600 per month, far out of her reach.

At Grace, Watson learned her blood sugar is high and that she needed to lose weight. Now, she walks laps around her backyard pool and does Tai Chi YouTube tutorials to focus on fitness. She said she wishes everyone could have her experience.

"It's very hard out here," she said. "It's not enough."

At the clinic, patients cycle in and out of a wide hallway lined with appointment rooms as doctors scan supply shelves for complimentary over-the-counter medications. The expansive building has separate areas for dental, mental health, vision and pediatric care.

CEO Stephanie Garris said it's one of 110 free or charitable clinics in Florida, but that's not enough to handle demand. To treat more people in response to the Affordable Care Act changes, it recently started hosting a mobile acute care clinic for walk-in patients.

Garris said Grace Medical Home treated about 1,350 people last year. Every year, they take about 350 new patients.

"Would I love to double that, triple that? Of course," Garris said. "I just think in the reality, with the huge number of uninsured that we have, it's just not possible."

Health costs become an issue in midterm campaigns

For U.S. Rep. Darren Soto, a Democrat defending his seat in a sprawling — and now much redder — redrawn district south of Orlando, health costs are a campaign focal point.

He said his district, which is near various theme parks, had the second-largest Affordable Care Act enrollment in the nation, in part because many small tourism businesses can't offer employees health insurance.

"I just hear it everywhere I go," he said. His Republican opponent, Navy veteran and former Trump administration official Dan Green, did not answer emailed questions about the subsidies but has emphasized affordability of groceries and property insurance as campaign priorities.

Soto voted with Democrats and some Republicans — including a few from Florida — to save the subsidies last year. The Republican majority declined and suggested other ideas, including funding Americans' health savings accounts. No law along those lines has passed yet.

Button, a Democrat in Soto's district, said he is open to different reforms for health costs, but said politicians aren't acting fast enough.

"They keep trying to make excuse after excuse," he said. "I don't have six months to a year to wait for you guys to pass this through the hoops that you need to."

articles.title: Is AIPAC’s political standing declining in the US?
articles.summary: The powerful pro-Israeli lobby group is increasingly becoming liability for both the progressive and the right wing.
articles.body:
Republican Mike Rogers and his allies have reportedly asked the pro-Israel lobby American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) not to run a campaign on his behalf ahead of the November midterm elections in the United States.

Rogers, who is a Republican Senate candidate from Michigan — home to one of the country’s largest Arab-American populations — fears that open AIPAC support might backfire.

list 2 of 3 Israel, Turkiye and the post-Abrahamic Middle East

list 3 of 3 Why is Israel building new illegal settlements?

According to US media reports, the request to the pro-Israel lobby came after Rogers met the AIPAC chair, Michael Tuchin, in Los Angeles last week.

This comes as the powerful pro-Israel lobby group has been facing mounting pressure from the progressive wing of the Democratic Party, which has been largely critical of Israel and its ongoing genocidal war on Gaza.

But now even Republican Party candidates are looking to distance themselves from the group as a growing number of Americans, both on the left and the right, have started to challenge US support for Israel.

So, what is AIPAC and why is an increasing number of US politicians refusing to receive its support?

AIPAC is officially a nonpartisan group that advocates unconditional US support for Israel and pushes back against any criticism of Israeli governments and their human rights record .

It was established in 1954, originally known as the American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs.

Its founding objective was to persuade Congress to fund Israel’s economy and the absorption of Jewish refugees, and it was framed as a US national interest rather than a special-interest favour.

After the 1967 Six-Day War and the 1973 Arab-Israeli War, its focus widened to military aid, advocating before US Congress members for military aid and joint defence cooperation for Israel.

AIPAC itself gave nothing to electoral candidates until the early 1980s, when it began using a network of separately incorporated pro-Israel political action committees (PACs), private groups that pool contributions from people and donate them to political campaigns.

That funding has been bipartisan, with AIPAC wielding significant influence in both parties; that was until a split emerged among Democrats, with progressives such as Rashida Tlaib and Ilhan Omar entering Congress around 2018 and pushing to condition military aid on human rights compliance.

In December 2021, it changed strategy, directly spending through AIPAC PAC and AIPAC-affiliated Super PAC United Democracy Project (UDP).

Super PACs are funded by individuals, unions and corporations and can donate unlimited amounts to independent organisations linked to a candidate.

AIPAC said the shift was forced by a changed Washington, with its then-president Betsy Berns Korn, citing hyperpartisanship, high congressional turnover and the exponential growth in campaign costs.

AIPAC has focused on Democratic primaries in liberal-leaning congressional districts, as it has since the 2022 primaries, when progressives are more likely to succeed.

Track AIPAC, an organisation that records the group’s funding of US politicians, has revealed that AIPAC spent more than $6m on just one Democratic candidate, Melissa Hernandez, who ran and lost against progressive Democrat California state Senator Aisha Wahab in a special election in California’s 14th district.

UDP alone raised about $104m during the 2026 cycle, according to factcheck.org, a nonpartisan, nonprofit website, $87.1m more than it collected during the 2024 cycle.

In Michigan’s Senate Democratic primary alone, it spent more than $30m backing four-term Congress member Haley Stevens against Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former public health official.

It is the most AIPAC has ever spent on one contest.

Despite this, El-Sayed, who focused on healthcare for all and the Palestinian cause, won the primary election and will face Rogers in the November election.

AIPAC has used shell PACs to obscure its spending in Democratic primaries.

In the Michigan Democratic primaries, a newly formed group PAC called A Stronger Michigan donated $17m. The PAC has been mostly bankrolled by a nonprofit, Center Forward, whose stated mission is to foster partisanship.

A Stronger Michigan has also received funds from another PAC that was established this year, Michigan Forward 2026.

In mid-March, during elections in Illinois, AIPAC used three different PACs to advertise to boost congressional candidate Bushra Amiwala and siphon off votes from more viable progressive candidates – namely, Palestinian-American activist Kat Abughazaleh , who ended up losing the race narrowly.

AIPAC still wields enormous influence in US politics.

Aid packages to Israel continue to pass by wide margins, and it still boasts the largest war chest of any single-issue lobby in Washington.

However, when it comes to recent efforts to sway US election results in favour of candidates who support Israel, AIPAC has faced setbacks.

Part of the backlash has come from broader public disillusionment with Israel-backed policies, including the US-Israel war on Iran and the genocide in Gaza, which AIPAC supports.

Some politicians who previously received support from the group are now disavowing it.

Last October, Democrat Congressman Seth Moulton distanced himself from AIPAC, citing the group’s support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The lawmaker announced he would also return donations from AIPAC.

“In recent years, AIPAC has aligned itself too closely with Prime Minister Netanyahu’s government,” Moulton had said in a statement.

“I’m a friend of Israel, but not of its current government, and AIPAC’s mission today is to back that government. I don’t support that direction. That’s why I’ve decided to return the donations I’ve received, and I will not be accepting their support.”

According to The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research survey conducted in June, 58 percent of Democrats said the US is too supportive of Israel, up from 45 percent in January 2024; 60 percent of Republicans said the US support is “about right”.

But as Israel continues with its genocidal war on Gaza and military operation in south Lebanon, AIPAC has also begun losing support from Republican candidates.

Besides Rogers’s recent request to the group, last August, AIPAC accused right-wing Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene of betraying “American values” over her criticism of Israel .

Greene shot back , saying AIPAC serves the interests of a foreign government. “I’m as AMERICAN as they come! I can’t be bought, and I’m not backing down,” she wrote in a social media post.

AIPAC has, however, repeatedly rejected the notion that it is a lobby group that serves a foreign government.

Instead, the organisation has presented itself as a coalition of engaged Americans who view a close US-Israel alliance as beneficial for both countries.

“As proud, pro-Israel Americans, we will never apologise for participating in the political process and standing up to those who undermine our shared values,” the group said in a recent email to supporters that listed the Senate race in Michigan as “critical”.

articles.title: Trump says US considering renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America
articles.summary: Trump's remarks come amid a deepening cross-border trade feud that has increasingly centered on Ontario Premier Doug Ford.
articles.body:
Minister of Industry of Canada, Mélanie Joly, has responded to President Donald Trump's comments that the United States is giving "serious consideration" to renaming Lake Ontario as "Lake America."

"We'll always call it Lake Ontario," Joly told reporters on Tuesday when asked about Trump's statement, the latest escalation in his increasingly bitter dispute with Canada as trade talks between the two countries remain stalled. "We're proud of the Great Lakes… and we'll stand up for what we have," she said. "I really think that, with all these shenanigans happening. We'll just be smart and we'll be strategic, and we'll fight back."

In a Tuesday post on Truth Social, Trump had suggested the move was under consideration because the U.S. did not expect to be "doing much business with Ontario any longer." The president later shared on his social-media platform a map of the lake with its current name crossed out and replaced with "Lake America." The proposal lands as relations between Washington and Ottawa are under fresh strain following the breakdown of trade talks and months of sparring between Trump and Ontario Premier Doug Ford.

"It is quite possible that Canadians could see the appropriation of Lake Ontario and its renaming as part of the larger effort on the part of the U.S. to exert its influence territorially," Derek Alderman, a cultural and historical geographer, told Newsweek . He added that the move seemed intended "to exert some advantage or strength in the trade war with Canada."

Meanwhile, Reuben Rose-Redwood, Professor of Geography at the University of Victoria, called it "pure rage bait" and a "well-worn move from the Trump playbook akin to calling Canada the '51st State' or renaming the Gulf of Mexico to capture media attention."

"Trump's threat to rename Lake Ontario is pure rage bait aimed at stoking anger among Canadians while distracting Americans from the fact that Trump overplayed his hand in the trade negotiations with Canada," he told Newsweek .

The official White House X account later shared a map of the United States, in the style of Lego, which labelled the lake which borders New York as "Lake America."

However, it appears that the map is incorrect with D.C. labeled as being located in North Carolina in the White House's map.

"How much drinking water did you idiots use up just to put DC and NJ in the wrong places?" The Lincoln Project asked in response to the post on X, referring to the assumption that the map was created via AI.

Minister of Industry of Canada Mélanie Joly says "we'll always call it Lake Ontario" in response to Trump's threat to rename it "Lake America" pic.twitter.com/Md9OH9hwNr — CSPAN (@cspan) August 25, 2026

Minister of Industry of Canada Mélanie Joly says "we'll always call it Lake Ontario" in response to Trump's threat to rename it "Lake America" pic.twitter.com/Md9OH9hwNr

Newsweek has contacted Ford's office and the office of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney for comment.

The White House referred Newsweek to Trump's Truth Social post when approached for clarification on his proposal.

The president's remarks come following the breakdown of trade talks between U.S. and Canadian negotiators on Friday.

Carney said last-minute changes by the American side were "unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," while U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer blamed Canada for the breakdown and told CNBC's Squawk Box that Ottawa's negotiators sought their own 11th-hour additions.

The U.S. has now imposed 50 percent tariffs on hundreds of Canadian products —targeting certain motor vehicles, alcoholic beverages, and dairy, as well as a host of other goods together worth around $20 billion—and Trump has threatened the same duties on Canadian cars, automotive parts and steel.

Prime Minister Carney has said the country will match these "dollar for dollar," and Ottawa is preparing to announce a specific set of countermeasures as soon as Tuesday which will come into effect in September.

Ford has emerged as one of the most vocal opponents of the administration's Canada policies. Ford has previously threatened trade retaliation and restriction s affecting exports to the U.S., making Ontario a frequent focus of Trump's criticism as tensions between the neighboring countries intensify.

Ford has said that his country was prepared for "an economic war." He told the Associated Press that "everything was on the table" when it came to responding to the new tariffs, including limiting restricting electricity exports and critical mineral supplies from Ontario.

Ford made a similar threat early last year, shortly after Trump's return to office and following the announcement of tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China.

The cross-border trade feud between the historic allies has often centered on Ford, who on Monday called Trump a dictator and said during a news conference in Hamilton that the U.S. president could "kiss my a**."

📍 Lake America pic.twitter.com/zqDh8pXkoq — The White House (@WhiteHouse) August 25, 2026

📍 Lake America pic.twitter.com/zqDh8pXkoq

— The White House (@WhiteHouse) August 25, 2026

Lake Ontario is one of North America's five Great Lakes, sitting on the U.S.-Canada border between Ontario and New York. It is the smallest Great Lake by surface area but serves as a key shipping link between the Great Lakes region and the Atlantic Ocean through the St. Lawrence Seaway. Major cities on its shores include Toronto, Hamilton and Rochester.

The city derives its name from the lake, which got it from an indigenous word predating both Canada and the United States. It is usually traced to the Wyandot (Huron) word Ontarí'io or a related Iroquoian term, variously translated as "great" or "beautiful" water.

Rose-Redwood said that while the Trump administration can order the name to be changed on U.S. federal maps, it has no power over whether Canada or international map makers do so. The last time Trump announced he was altering the name of a location, the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America, other countries failed to follow suit.

"Trump can certainly instruct the U.S. Department of the Interior and the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to rename Lake Ontario on U.S. federal maps, yet Canadian and international mapmakers are not obliged to comply with any decrees coming from the White House," Rose-Redwood told Newsweek .

"Although President Trump's threat of a name change is meant to exert some advantage or strength in the trade war with Canada that has ensued, it actually could backfire by further alienating the Canadian people," said Alderman, a former president of the American Association of Geographers. "Place names are quite important to people's identity as well as key resources in educating our youth and being key parts of treaties, policy documents and maps used for a variety of economic and political activities."

Alderman, now a professor in the University of Tennessee's Geography & Sustainability Department, told Newsweek that such a change would only exacerbate fears that Trump is hoping to turn the country into a "51st state," while also threatening Canadian identity.

"On a deeper level, the president's abrupt and unilateral threat to rename Lake Ontario, seemingly without proper public discussion or governmental deliberation, would say something negative about how the names on our maps, landscapes and bodies of water are being reduced to pawns and weapons in the latest battles over trade negotiation and insults traded between U.S. and Canadian leaders," he added.

The proposal would also create an unexpected classroom headache. Generations of students have memorized the Great Lakes using the acronym "HOMES" for Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie and Superior. A different name for Lake Ontario would render the mnemonic obsolete.

The name Lake Ontario predates both the United States and Canada and has Indigenous origins.

The name is generally traced to an Iroquoian term, often rendered as Ontarí'io or Ontario , which has been interpreted as meaning "great lake" or "beautiful water." The precise linguistic origin and meaning have been debated, but the name was in use long before European settlement and eventually became the name used for the lake and the province of Ontario.

That history gives the proposed name change an additional cultural dimension. Lake Ontario is not simply a label on a modern map: its name is connected to Indigenous languages and centuries of history in the Great Lakes region.

The lake's name was subsequently adopted by the province of Ontario, which was established as a British North American province in 1867 and later became Canada's most populous province.

A move by the U.S. to refer to the lake as "Lake America" on federal maps would therefore place a modern political label over a name with a much longer history.

Lake Ontario is the smallest of the five Great Lakes by surface area, but it is considerably deeper than its size might suggest.

The lake has an average depth of approximately 283 feet and reaches a maximum depth of about 802 feet. It covers roughly 7,340 square miles with about one-quarter of its surface area in the United States and the remainder in Canada.

Lake Ontario is also an important part of the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence waterway. Water from the other Great Lakes flows through Lake Ontario before continuing down the St. Lawrence River toward the Atlantic Ocean.

Its shores include major population centers including Toronto, Hamilton and Kingston in Ontario, as well as Rochester and Oswego in New York.

The lake's geography also underscores why a change to its name would have consequences beyond a map label. Lake Ontario is a major international waterway, forming part of the border between two countries and supporting shipping, tourism, fishing, industry and millions of people living around its shores.

List of Places Trump Has Renamed Since Returning to Office

Trump's suggestion that Lake Ontario could become "Lake America" would be the latest example of his efforts to rename or rebrand prominent geographic features since returning to office. In 2025, he ordered federal agencies to adopt the name "Gulf of America" in place of the Gulf of Mexico and restored Mount McKinley as the federal name for Alaska's Denali, reversing a 2015 Obama-era change.

The president has also shown a willingness to use provocative place-naming proposals as a political statement. Earlier this month, he shared an image on Truth Social depicting the Strait of Hormuz as "NEW U.S. Territory" and publicly entertained the idea of asserting U.S. control over the strategically important waterway.

While it remains unclear whether any formal effort will be made to rename Lake Ontario, the proposal fits a broader pattern of Trump using symbolic geographic branding to advance political messages, particularly in disputes involving trade, national identity and U.S. influence abroad.

articles.title: Bessent slow rolls ‘Economic D-Day’ on Iran
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Voters head to polls in GOP runoffs ▪ Supreme Court upholds mail-in order for now ▪ Trump threatens another round of Canada tariffs ▪ Nevada sues over Colorado River use cuts Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent rolled out the Trump administration’s much-anticipated “Economic D-Day” offensive against Iran on Monday but signaled the plan entails more of…
articles.body:
▪ Supreme Court upholds mail-in order for now

▪ Trump threatens another round of Canada tariffs

▪ Nevada sues over Colorado River use cuts

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent rolled out the Trump administration’s much-anticipated “Economic D-Day” offensive against Iran on Monday but signaled the plan entails more of a threat than immediately bringing the hammer down, at least for now.

Bessent issued a warning during a press conference for all countries to cut off business and other financial ties with Iran or else face significant sanctions.

The plan has been named “Operation Economic Outcast” and promoted as comparable to the U.S. invasion of Normandy during World War II. But Bessent avoided naming specific countries that the U.S. is seeking to pressure and didn’t share many specific actions or a timeline that the federal government would take.

“Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior, why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he said, when asked at a press conference why sanctions wouldn’t take effect immediately.

Bessent said diplomacy is happening behind the scenes, as President Trump is calling world leaders to get them to cut off Iran. He said officials from the State, Treasury and Defense departments are also calling their counterparts around the world.

He expressed confidence about the plan, saying that the U.S. has “already seen some results” and emphasizing that Trump can be “quite persuasive.”

But the announcement fell short of quite the boisterous threats that the president has been making for days leading up to the move, as he seeks to force Iran back to the bargaining table and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

“Therefore, today, I am announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY!” Trump said in a Truth Social post Wednesday. “This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale.”

Trump said any country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities to provide “any type of lifeline” to Iran will face “TREMENDOUS” economic consequences.

While the president hasn’t ruled out additional military action against Iran, he has shifted his focus to the economic realm amid growing warnings over depleted U.S. weapons stockpiles.

One complicating factor to the “outcast” plan is the role of China, which is Iran’s largest trading partner. Bessent said “no country is above the reach of U.S. sanctions” when asked plans for China.

Experts told NBC News that the success of Bessent’s announcement will depend on whether Iran’s most powerful trading partners — China, India and Russia — deem the U.S. threats credible.

Bessent also announced other actions designed to squeeze Iran economically, including placing sanctions on 60 entities, individuals and vessels related to Iran’s nuclear and missile technology programs, its ability to conduct cyber operations and generate oil revenue.

The Treasury Department said it was expanding its authority to sanction any person, regardless of location, for operating specific sectors of the Iranian economy, including digital assets, technology, aviation and shipping.

Iran’s currency, the rial, continued to take a hit on Monday, falling to a record low of about 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar. U.S. markets seemed to mostly shrug at the news, as the Dow Jones finished slightly up compared to the start of the day, while Nasdaq and the S&P 500 finished slightly lower.

Signs of Iran’s economic struggles amid the war continue to multiply. The International Monetary Fund said its economy will contract by 5.4 percent this year, while the government is signaling a coming hike to fuel prices in a bid to buoy the economy, a move that will compound rising prices.

What’s less certain is whether that pain is increasing pressure on the hardline regime to end the war.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf , who has led negotiations with the U.S., have pointed to the economic anxiety in remarks about the country’s war posture in recent days.

However, leaders of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps are seen as digging in, promoting a more assertive approach to the war focused on “offensive operations.”

An adviser to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said the “strategy of shifting the war to an offensive posture if Iran’s conditions are not met will undoubtedly transform the balance of power in the world,” CNN reported.

How much Iran’s military is willing to test that theory, or whether the U.S. is willing to put the screws to global powers still supporting Iran, are key questions in a war that has now gone on for almost six months.

Republican California gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton revealed to NewsNation his plan to try to stop parents and teachers from having to pick up the cost of school supplies. It’s another way to address the affordability issue . As we saw last week, Trump had his own idea regarding importing beef to lower prices for consumers. However, American ranchers have panned the plan. So did Hilton when I spoke with him on Monday.

“I’m not a fan of that policy at all. I’ve been with our ranchers across the state, and they are really struggling,” Hilton told me . He also pointed the finger at Democrats. “The struggle in California is because of California policies, the regulations that they have to comply with, way more onerous than other states,” he added.

Bringing down prices in any form remains a key issue for Republicans, whether it be in the meat section, or school supplies section, of your local grocery store.

By the way, we are bringing back our Viewer’s Voice segment on Wednesday. Have a question for Congress? Email me at viewersvoice@newsnationnow.com . We’ll put your questions to Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-Md.).

Burman hosts “The Hill” weeknights, 6 p.m. EDT/5 p.m. CDT on NewsNation.

The federal government is reportedly planning to revoke the visas for up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are seeking asylum in the U.S. If the move goes through, it would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in U.S. history.

The Trump administration formally removed Syria from the state sponsor of terrorism list , a significant milestone for the country as its government under Ahmad al-Sharaa seeks to restore ties with the international community. The move will allow Damascus to fully rejoin the global financial system.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) assured the public that no one in the president’s circle would “get a pass” if Democrats win back control of the House in November. His comments came in response to some backlash to his reported meeting with Jared Kushner to discuss areas of common ground with the administration.

President Trump watches Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) speak at her campaign event at the Myrtle Beach Convention Center in Myrtle Beach, S.C., Aug. 21, 2026. (Mic Smith, Associated Press)

RUNOFFS : Tonight’s primaries will provide two of the final major tests of Trump’s endorsement power in this year’s midterm primaries.

Trump has weighed into today’s GOP primary runoffs for South Carolina’s Senate seat and for Oklahoma’s governorship, expending political capital in two races that are anyone’s to win.

In South Carolina, Trump has thrown his weight behind Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), who is serving out the final months of her late brother’s term as she seeks a full six-year term of her own. She faces Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.), a longtime member of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus who is leaning on his experience in office.

Graham and Norman advanced to a runoff after earning about 33 percent and 25 percent, respectively, in the Aug. 11 special primary, setting off a two-week sprint to today’s runoff.

But without much public polling — and after Graham’s fumble over a national security question during last week’s debate — the race is up for grabs. One poll released late Monday night showed the race essentially tied .

Over in Oklahoma , Trump’s pick, Republican Mike Mazzei , finished less than a percentage point behind his opponent, Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond (R), who was viewed as an early favorite in the race before Trump weighed in just two weeks before the June primary.

Drummond has faced the president’s ire over his resistance to a Trump-backed project to bring what would be the country’s largest aluminum smelter to his state and filed a suit to block the plant, arguing it would hurt residents and their land. Trump has also suggested Drummond was not supportive enough during his impeachment trials.

The president joined back-to-back tele-rallies last night with each candidate as he urged voters to turn out to the polls.

▪ The Hill Insider : Graham hopes Trump propels her across finish line.

▪ The Hill : Drummond says Trump is ‘wrong’ on tariffs.

SCOTUS SURPRISE : The Supreme Court has lifted a federal judge’s block on Trump’s executive order implementing requirements for mail-in voting, with the majority finding that a handful of Democratic-leaning state sued too early for courts to weigh in.

The conservative majority ruled over the dissents of the court’s three liberals that the judge didn’t have the authority to block the order before the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) implements the new standards.

The ruling allows the president to move closer to instituting his order ahead of the midterms. Trump signed the order in March to direct his administration to create a list of verified citizens who are eligible to vote and for USPS to only send ballots to citizens on a state’s approved mail-in ballot list.

California, Massachusetts, Nevada and Washington co-led the lawsuit challenging the order, leading a total of nearly two dozen states and Washington, D.C.

The ruling covers the timing of the case but not the merits. Additional legal challenges may be to come, leaving whether the order can be implemented in time for November uncertain.

▪ The Hill : Justice Department signals appeal coming on Epstein files redactions.

NEXT ROUND : Trump is already looking ahead to implementing another wave of steep tariffs on Canada following Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ’s announcement that his government will impose retaliatory tariffs against the U.S.

The president threatened Monday that he would place additional 50 percent tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts and steel starting Jan. 1. That would be on top of the 50 percent tariffs that went into effect at the end of last week on a range of Canadian goods, including wine, furniture and cement.

Carney’s retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods — including dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment and electronics — will take effect Sept. 8.

Trade talks between the countries collapsed at the end of last week. Carney has said the U.S.’s terms were unacceptable, including a late demand that restrictions be placed on Canada’s ability to reach trade deals with other countries.

Trump administration officials have accused Canada of being the one making last-minute changes, with the president saying on Truth Social on Monday that Canada has been “ripping off” the U.S. for years.

▪ The Hill Insider : What to know about US-Canada trade war impacts.

▪ The Hill Insider : Tariff war threatens GOP candidates in border battlegrounds.

TRY TRY AGAIN :The Trump administration is again planning to charge employers more than $100,000 for skilled international workers they hire through the H-1B work visa program, according to a notice of proposed rulemaking issued Monday by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

A federal judge in June struck down the Trump administration’s proposal for a $100,000 fee for H-1B visa applications, ruling only Congress could levy taxes and set immigration laws.

But DHS’s proposed rule indicates that the fee would function as a “dedicated revenue mechanism” to recover some of the cost of administering the immigration system.

“The proposed H ‑ 1B fee is intended to recover the costs incurred across the federal government to adjudicate, vet, and support lawful immigration programs that otherwise must be funded by taxpayers,” U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services spokesperson Zach Kahler said in a release.

▪ The Hill : Texas governor fights Minnesota extradition request for immigration officer.

The president will participate in a pre-taped interview at 2 p.m. He will participate in signing time at 4 p.m.

A grocery store worker prepares to display ground beef for purchase in Dallas, April 15, 2026. (LM Otero, Associated Press)

INTRAPARTY BEEF : Senate Republicans are breaking with the president over his plan to pause tariffs on beef imports as he escalates duties on key Canadian products.

The Hill’s Alexander Bolton reports several Republicans from agriculture-heavy states are urging Trump against the plan to exempt 300,000 tons of product for ground beef from out-of-quote tariffs.

Trump decided to use the pause to address consumers’ worries about rising food costs, but the Republicans said they’re concerned about cheap beef imports flooding the market in the coming months.

“They’re skating where the puck is versus where it needs to be. If you think that providing subsidized beef for some period of time is going to make farmers happy and prices go down on systemic basis, you’re wrong. It doesn’t happen,” said Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.).

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) brushed off Trump’s move as a “quick fix,” while Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.), a member of the Agriculture Committee, said the relatively strong beef prices are a “bright spot” for a “struggling” agricultural industry.

Bolton reports Trump seems to be sensitive to ground beef costs, which have risen about 20 percent since he took office last January. Some Democratic candidates, including Iowa Senate candidate Josh Turek , are emphasizing “skyrocketing” beef prices while campaigning.

Trump has vowed that imported beef will be sold at 25 percent below current market prices over the next three months. But many Republicans said allowing cheap imports isn’t the best solution.

▪ The Hill : Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) calls Canada tariffs a ‘mistake.’

▪ NewsNation : Why farmers oppose Trump’s plan to import beef.

The Colorado River flows near the Glen Canyon Dam, Tuesday, July 14, 2026, near Page, Nev. (AP Photo/John Locher)

WATER FIGHT: Nevada is suing the federal government over its finalized plan to force certain states to reduce their Colorado River water usage over the next 10 years, saying the cuts are too steep and could threaten people’s health and safety and devastate local economies.

“This isn’t about political posturing; this is a matter of survival for a community that represents about two-thirds of our state’s citizens and the lion’s share of its economy,” Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) said in a statement.

The Colorado River provides water for agricultural, municipal and industrial uses for seven states: Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming.

The river has been facing a major drought and, as the climate gets drier, the states have had to negotiate the river’s future management, especially since the interim guidelines expire at the end of the year.

But, after the states failed to reach an agreement, the federal government had to step in, and last month, the Interior Department released a 10-year framework that would force California, Arizona and Nevada to cut up to 3 million acre-feet per year.

The three states recoiled at the proposal, and the Interior Department responded with a short-term plan that would instead require the three states to reduce their water use by 1.25 million acre-feet per year in 2027 and 2028.

But the department on Friday also finalized the 10-year plan, which the Trump administration has said is meant to be a flexible framework that is responsive to whatever the water conditions may be in the future.

▪ The Arizona Republic : Is Arizona next to sue?

▪ The Associated Press : Firefighters make progress against Nevada wildfire.

South Carolina runoff pits America First against MAGA , The Hill’s Chris Stirewalt writes .

The FCC’s power over broadcasters was a mistake from the start , Dominic Pino writes in The Washington Post.

And finally … Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas thanked Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) for standing up for him in the face of ethics complaints in recent years when the judge appeared on an episode of Cruz’s podcast released Monday.

“You’re one of the people who actually stands up, particularly at times when others seem to wither, and I appreciate it,” Thomas said on the episode of “Verdict with Ted Cruz.”

Thomas has faced scrutiny in recent years over allegations that he failed to disclose gifts, luxury travel and property transactions involving billionaire Harlan Crow , a GOP megadonor. He’s also faced criticism over perceived conflicts of interest given political activism from his wife, Ginni Thomas .

“That is very kind of you, and especially for you to observe that I stand up in the face of criticism and attacks, that is powerful coming from you because you’re someone who knows what that’s like and has done so in a way that has been world-changing,” Cruz responded.

articles.title: The victory lap on Trump’s nuclear campus plan is premature
articles.summary: Before anyone declares the gridlock is broken, the plan should clear five tests.
articles.body:
In late July, the Department of Energy announced that five states — Utah, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Louisiana and Idaho — had agreed to explore hosting Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses .

Energy Secretary Chris Wright called the campuses “massive generators of economic growth” that would be “crucial to unleashing America’s nuclear renaissance.” The American Nuclear Society echoed him, its president promising “multigenerational job creation, sustained economic growth, and new investment in education and workforce development.”

By folding nuclear waste into a sweeping economic development package, the department has invited states to compete for campuses that could co-locate multiple stages of the nuclear fuel cycle — such as uranium enrichment, fuel fabrication, spent fuel reprocessing, waste disposition and, in some states, advanced reactors. This is all while using the appeal of nuclear power investment to soften the politics of hosting long-term waste facilities.

It is an appealing vision. But five signed memoranda are not five host communities. No final host agreement has been signed, no construction funds awarded and the states have agreed only to continue negotiations. That is a real beginning, but it is not a victory. Treating it as one risks repeating the cycle of overpromising and disappointment that has paralyzed American nuclear waste policy for four decades.

I say this as a former Energy Department official who served as federal manager for the Consent-Based Siting Consortia — a $24 million 12-team initiative supporting public engagement around the siting of spent-fuel storage facilities. Before anyone declares the gridlock is broken, the plan must clear five tests.

First, the department must explain the scale of its projections. Its January solicitation offered an illustrative scenario in which one campus employed 50,000 direct workers, generated another 100,000 to 150,000 indirect jobs, and required 10,000 to 20,000 housing units. The same document put the entire existing U.S. nuclear workforce at roughly 80,000. By July, the Energy Department was projecting 25,000 jobs per campus .

Those figures may rest on different assumptions, but the Energy Department has not explained the methodology or reconciled the difference. Numbers that swing this far before a single site is chosen are aspirations, not plans.

Second, the department needs a technically credible schedule. Its solicitation says it wants initial facilities online “in the 2027 timeframe” and promises preference to the states with “more ambitious timelines” — remarkably soon for infrastructure of this kind.

States, meanwhile, had just nine weeks to assemble sweeping proposals. Any serious schedule for the waste disposition component must separately account for geological screening, independent site characterization, groundwater and seismic studies, environmental review, Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensing, transportation planning and host-agreement negotiation. A facility built to isolate waste for decades, centuries, or millennia cannot be validated on a ribbon-cutting schedule.

Third, Washington must put up real money and enforceable commitments. A repository would, in principle, draw on the federal Nuclear Waste Fund . But for nearly everything else, the department told states to look to private capital — industry, technology firms, private equity, venture funds. It floats possible federal cost-sharing, loan guarantees and grants, but it commits to none and says states and private investors are expected to lead and finance the effort.

Communities asked to keep nuclear waste for generations need money that is committed and obligations that are enforceable against future administrations.

Fourth, Congress must authorize the plan’s spent-fuel storage and disposal components. The Nuclear Waste Policy Act still directs the federal repository program toward Yucca Mountain, whose development Congress has not funded since fiscal 2010 . The act also prevents construction of a centralized federal spent fuel storage facility until the Nuclear Regulatory Commission has authorized construction of a repository. The department cannot designate one of the five states as a spent fuel site by press release.

Fifth, host communities must consent. States applied and governors signed, and some local governments in Utah, Idaho and Tennessee have expressed preliminary support. But it is far from clear that any specific community has agreed to live beside nuclear waste facilities.

Genuine consent requires a named candidate community, early involvement rather than after-the-fact persuasion, meaningful say over benefits, the participation of affected Tribal Nations and a real chance to walk away before commitments are final. The Energy Department’s process ran the other way: It gave states nine weeks to name sites and gauge local sentiment and rewarded those promising to streamline permitting and move fast.

After decades in which states treated nuclear waste as politically untouchable, the willingness of five governors to enter the negotiating room is a real achievement. But no spent-fuel repository in any of the five states is authorized under current law, no community has completed a voluntary siting process, no binding host agreement has been signed and no durable financing package or credible schedule has been demonstrated.

When a willing community stays at the table through investigation, negotiation, licensing and construction, the Energy Department will have earned its victory lap. For now, it has earned only the right to begin the hard work of getting there.

Vincent Ialenti is a former U.S. Department of Energy official and a senior research fellow at Tampere University in Finland. He is the author of “Deep Time Reckoning” and “Longstorming,” both from MIT Press.

articles.body:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (QUEEN CITY NEWS) — Manolo Bentancur is talking about the conversation he had with the former commander of U.S. Border Patrol, Greg Bovino , when Bentancur saw Bovino at his popular east Charlotte bakery Sunday afternoon.

“He said, ‘Well, I can be wherever I want; it’s free,” said Bentancur. “I said, ‘This is private property; you are not allowed on this property. There’s a lot of fear of you, a lot of fear of ICE, and a lot of fear over what is going on in our nation.'”

Bovino and a cameraman were spotted in the parking lot of the bakery when Bentancur arrived to pick up his wife from work.

Last November, Bovino led Operation Charlotte’s Web , a federal immigration enforcement sweep that resulted in over 1,300 arrests, with much of the activity starting in the parking lot of Manolo’s bakery.

“‘Ah, you’re Manolo, you are the owner,'” Bentancur says Bovino told him. “‘You are the one who shut the business down in November so you can protect all the illegals that are here.'”

Queen City News reached out to Gregory Bovino, and he tells us that’s not what happened in the parking lot. In a written statement, Bovino says he never tried to enter the bakery. Bovino went on to say he was recording video of businesses from Operation Charlotte’s Web when his videographer asked to buy something in the bakery, and Bentancur declined.

“It’s not like he came to walk inside the bakery; ‘No,’ I told him if you are thinking about going inside the bakery, you are not going to go inside,” added Bentancur.

Bovino says he asked Bentancur, “Why he would choose an illegal alien over an American citizen and he was unable to answer.”

Bentancur says this interaction shows how his community and businesses in east Charlotte remain under attack. From bad reviews of his bakery to someone recently throwing eggs at the business, the hate speech keeps increasing.

“I have been prepared since November about what I am going to be reacting, what I am going to be saying the day I had to face these people, but I never thought it would be Bovino man,” said Bentancur.

Gregory Bovino says he plans to post the entire video of the interaction online later this week.

Action NC, a non-profit advocacy group, shared a statement following Bovino’s visit calling his actions “reprehensible” and an “attempt at intimidation tactics.”

“ They can only be described as an attempt by a man who perceives himself to be strong attempting to intimidate a business in a community that he perceives to be weaker. What he encountered showed the opposite. He was immediately told he was not welcome and made to leave ,” the group said.

Action NC Immigrant Justice Director, Héctor Vaca, added, “ We applaud Manolo and support his business. He is the type of leader that our community needs more of. He not only talks the talk, he walks it and strongly defends those that feel disempowered in the current climate created by people like Bovino. We call on all of Charlotte to show its love and support a business that supports its community. ”

The group praises Bentancur, who is an Action NC member, calling him “a community leader that builds and supports his community” and “a model of what a good leader should be–kind, generous, empowering others, advocate, hardworking.”

articles.summary: Merrill Matthews argues that Sen. Bernie Sanders’ “Medicare for All” proposal deceptively seeks to replace the highly-rated existing Medicare program with a centralized, government-run system modeled after the United Kingdom’s less efficient National Health Service.
articles.body:
It may be one of the most deceptive public policy marketing schemes in modern history. First, pick the most popular health insurance program in the country, which is Medicare. Then call your health insurance reform proposal “ Medicare for All ,” even though the intent is to eliminate the Medicare program as we know it, so that no one would have that coverage anymore.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has long pushed to end the nation’s current mix of private health insurance (that is, employer-based and individually purchased) and government-provided health insurance (Medicare and Medicaid) and replace it with a new government-run program. Taxpayers would pay higher taxes — though no one would pay premiums — and the government would pay all medical bills.

Under most government-run health care systems, as in the United Kingdom , the government determines what services and medicines are available, who can have them and when. Bureaucrats rather than doctors decide whether patients are allowed to have access to those services and medicines.

That is what Sanders and 71 percent of Democrats mean by Medicare for All. But that’s not Medicare.

Sanders knows he’s being deceptive. His Senate website says , “Medicare is the most popular health care program in America.” Then he claims that under Medicare for All, “every resident of the U.S. will receive health insurance through an expanded Medicare program.” That is a blatantly false statement.

Medicare has multiple parts. Part A covers hospital bills, Part B covers doctors’ bills, Part C is now Medicare Advantage and Part D covers prescription drugs. Medicare for All has none of that.

Importantly, Medicare Advantage relies on private sector health insurance similar to employer plans. Seniors have a choice between traditional Medicare and Medicare Advantage . Currently, 55 percent of eligible seniors choose Medicare Advantage. Medicare for All excludes private sector coverage, including Medicare Advantage.

Remember President Obama’s promise for the Affordable Care Act? “If you like your health plan, you can keep it,” is what he said. That won him Politifact’s 2013 “Lie of the Year.” But Sanders won’t make that claim, because he intends to ensure no one has their current health plan, including people currently on Medicare.

A recent NBC News poll found that 82 percent are “satisfied with their health care coverage” and 90 percent of seniors on Medicare are satisfied with their plan, with 42 percent reporting they are “very satisfied.” But under Medicare for All, seniors can kiss their Medicare plan goodbye.

Medicare for All is more like the British National Health Service’s government-run health care system. Are the Brits as satisfied with their coverage as U.S. seniors are with Medicare? The 40-year running British Social Attitudes survey found last year that only 26 percent of British subjects are satisfied with the National Health Service, with 51 percent dissatisfied.

So, to recap, we’re going to take a system that has 90 percent satisfaction and abolish it in favor of one that has 26 percent satisfaction.

To be sure, Medicare is also a government-run program. It has many of the same problems as Great Britian’s system, including the very low rates it pays health care providers. When the government takes over the health care system, it must balance what it spends on health care with other claims on government funds, such as education, defense and welfare. There is never enough money to go around. That is why bureaucrats decide what medical services and products are available, usually based on political pressure.

Anyone who tracks the National Health Service’s problems knows this. It was a typical occurrence when officials warned last October about coming layoffs within the service unless funding was increased by £3bn “to cover unexpected costs.”

There are often long waiting lines to see a doctor — and very long lines to see a specialist. The NHS currently states on its website that it tries to cap waits for “non-urgent” treatment at “18 weeks from the day your appointment is booked” — so if you get a referral today, you might be treated in January. Also, many of the newest treatments and prescription drugs available in the U.S. are not available in Great Britain.

The Medicare program survives because most Americans are in private insurance plans, which essentially cross-subsidize Medicare. Health care providers make more from private-sector health insurers, allowing most of them to continue providing care for seniors on Medicare. That is far from ideal, but it is better than putting everyone into government-run health care.

Remember that when health care becomes political, the politically powerful — like members of Congress, including Sanders — and the well-connected will still get the care they want or need. Sanders won’t have to wait for care; you will.

Merrill Matthews is the Texas state chair of Our Republican Legacy.
